articles.title_orig: Apple Risks Losing the AI Agent War With an Outdated Playbook
articles.title_zh: Apple Risks Losing the AI Agent War With an Outdated Playbook
articles.content_orig:
Apple's recent Siri layoffs affected employees working on the assistant's older infrastructure rather than its newer AI underpinnings, according to Mark Gurman .
Smaller cuts across Siri, Vision Pro, and AI software teams were reported in September as CEO John Ternus pushed for leaner management and shorter development timelines. Affected hardware engineering program managers, including roughly half a dozen directors, were given weeks to find other roles at Apple.
iOS 27.3 beta 2 lets common Home and Intercom requests run on-device through new app actions instead of being handed back to the older Siri system.
Apple separately advertised an engineering role for a computer-use AI agent on November 17. The role involved work with Siri, user interface frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models on software that could navigate apps, browse websites, and write code. The posting was removed after drawing public attention, with Gurman noting the takedown on November 20.

articles.title_orig: Russell Brand’s wife vows to abide by prison rules after video controversy
articles.title_zh: Russell Brand’s wife vows to abide by prison rules after video controversy
articles.content_orig:
Laura Brand says in new video on YouTube she will continue Sunday Service series she started with Brand
Russell Brand’s wife, Laura, has promised to “absolutely honour” rules set by the prison where her convicted sex offender husband is being held, in another YouTube video published on Sunday.
This week Andy Burnham called on Google to take down a video uploaded to Russell Brand’s YouTube channel last Sunday that contained a statement from the disgraced comedian in prison, where he is serving a 10-and-a-half-year sentence for rape and sexual assaults.
Laura Brand began the latest episode of Sunday Service – described as a Christian series, which the couple started together six months ago – by telling viewers: “Last week’s episode drew considerable amount of attention and now that I understand the parameters set by the brilliant and professional staff at HMP Littlehey, I will absolutely honour that.”
She went on to address scrutiny regarding her continuing to run her husband’s YouTube channel, amid a Ministry of Justice inquiry focusing on whether Brand has broken rules that are supposed to prevent “serious distress” to the victims of crime.
“I am choosing to continue Sunday Service because I really enjoy it,” she said. “It is also a place where I will continue to be proud to be a wife, a mother and a woman defending her family at a time when the media’s image of what kind of a woman I am is under so much scrutiny.”
In the previous episode, the first published since Brand was jailed – after being convicted of one count of rape and three sexual assaults at Southwark crown court on 5 November – Laura Brand read out a message from him protesting that he was not guilty.
The video, titled “The Good Work Continues”, has remained on YouTube despite ministers repeatedly asking for it to be removed.
That video has now accumulated more than 1m views, becoming the best-performing video on Brand’s channel since 5 December last year, when he published a video conversation he had with the American conservative influencer Candace Owens. Many of his videos in the last year have drawn only between 50,000 and 100,000 views.
On Thursday night, Burnham said he “wouldn’t leap” to changing the law to force social media companies to take down such content. But he added: “I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down. You know, why are we having to hear from him? We shouldn’t be, and certainly [the victims] shouldn’t be hearing from him.”

articles.title_orig: Russian cargo ship leaves Finland’s territorial waters after drone attack
articles.title_zh: Russian cargo ship leaves Finland’s territorial waters after drone attack
articles.content_orig:
Russian ship engulfed in flames after explosion at Libyan port
An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.
The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libya state media reported, citing the eastern government.
The statement said there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.
Later on Sunday, the health ministry said it had received injured from another vessel, a commercial ship, that was also targeted off the coast of Benghazi, state media reported. Their injuries were minor and their condition stable, the ministry said.
Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port.
Satellite imagery showed a ship on fire at the port
US-based intelligence firm Vantor collected high-resolution images that it said showed Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette (Merkury) - a Russian navy ship - moored in the port on Saturday, and on Sunday showed most of the same ship capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible.
The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship - which it did not name or identify - was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.
GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.
Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.
GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".
Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.
Although it has not been officially confirmed who was behind the attack, there is little doubt, according to Jalel Harchaoui, Libya specialist at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).
"Ukraine is the only actor brazen enough to pull something like that off," he told the BBC. "If I were to bet my own money, I would bet that it was the Ukrainians."
If confirmed, it would not be the first time Ukrainian forces had carried out an operation of this sort. In March, Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the Russian tanker Arctic Metagaz in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta with "uncrewed sea drones" launched from the Libyan coast.
As well as having an economic impact on Russia, hampering the ability of their so-called shadow fleet of tankers to export oil and gas, attacks like this are seen as humiliating to the Kremlin, according to Harchaoui.
But it is not only Moscow that will want to react to this latest incident. The ship was in the region as part of a deal with the government of eastern Libya - allied with Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army.
Harchaoui said Haftar will take the attack as a personal slight. "You're going to have a response by the Haftar family. They will ask questions about who is hosting the Ukrainians."

articles.title_orig: Suspected Jewish settler extremist attack Palestinian towns across West Bank
articles.title_zh: Suspected Jewish settler extremist attack Palestinian towns across West Bank
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of militant Israeli settlers raided communities on Saturday night, setting fire to vehicles and several homes
Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank have caused a political row in Israel, drawing condemnation from Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader, who described them as “Jewish terrorism”.
Dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday, setting fire to about a dozen vehicles and several homes and scrawling racist graffiti. At least four communities were attacked. Israeli police said they had launched an investigation with forensic teams.
Photographs from Kafr Malik , near Ramallah, showed one slogan written in Hebrew that read: “This is the first revenge.” Several vehicles and homes had been set alight in the village.
Images from nearby Deir al-Sudan showed vehicles on fire. Palestinian reports said an agricultural building had been set ablaze in Deir Ballut and cars torched in Deir Abu Mashal.
An ⁠inconclusive election last month stripped Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, of his majority. Eisenkot has been asked to form a government, though his prospects seem little better.
“Last night’s arson attacks in Judea and Samaria were acts of Jewish terrorism, in every sense of the term,” Eisenkot said, using the biblical name for the West Bank. “Extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes are undermining regional stability, putting lives at risk and doing grave damage to Israel’s national security and foreign relations.”
Referring to the far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, he added: “The actions led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in the West Bank have brought the area to the brink of unchecked anarchy.”
Eisenkot, who has been given 28 days to form a government by the president, Isaac Herzog, with a possible 14-day extension, urged the government and security establishment to “use every tool at their disposal – including administrative detention and targeted operations by the Shin Bet – to stop the rioters and impose harsh sanctions on them”.
In an unprecedented rebuke on Sunday, several other members of the Israeli parliament criticised Netanyahu over escalating violence by militant settlers against Palestinians.
Yair Lapid, the leader of Yesh Atid, held Netanyahu’s government responsible for encouraging the attacks. “Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence by the Israeli government,” he said on X, adding that ministers were deliberately encouraging the militant settlers’ violence “through their silence”.
Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats party, warned of the possibility of a third intifada and described the West Bank as “on the brink of an explosion”.
“Anyone who wants to prevent a third intifada must replace the current government, which provides cover and support for Jewish terrorism and abandons security,” Golan said on X. “Jewish terrorism harms innocent Palestinians and Israeli army soldiers, and pushes Israel toward unprecedented international isolation.”
Noam Tibon, a retired army major general and Knesset member, gave a similar warning. “If Israel does not eliminate Jewish terrorism in the West Bank, it will destroy Israel,” he wrote.
Netanyahu has not yet responded to the accusations.
Australia announced sanctions on Wednesday against three people and four Israeli entities, including a construction company, over their role in the expansion of illegal settlements and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
A day earlier the UK imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building illegal settlements in the West Bank, which the UN regards as Palestinian territory under Israeli occupation since 1967.
Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.
On Tuesday, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli militant settlers in a village near Jericho, where the group has recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.
Reuters contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: Finance, fossil fuels and the ‘overshoot’: six key takeaways from Cop31
articles.title_zh: Finance, fossil fuels and the ‘overshoot’: six key takeaways from Cop31
articles.content_orig:
EU, UK and some of developing world object to main text that ‘failed to meet the moment’ and did not mention fossil fuels
The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey .
The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”
As the talks, scheduled to end on Friday, dragged on into Sunday afternoon in the longest climate summit ever, it was clear that the “Antalya pact”, drafted by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies of the summit, would not achieve the consensus needed to pass.
The Antalya pact invites countries to electrify their economies, calls for rich countries to provide finance to the poor to help them adapt to the impacts of the climate crisis, and calls on countries to minimise the “overshoot” of the 1.5C global heating threshold, of the Paris agreement.
But it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” that more than 130 countries demanded, and included controversial provisions on “carbon capture and storage” (CCS) technology that some have said perpetuates fossil fuels.
The presidencies avoided outright collapse of the “conference of the parties” by passing decisions on various related matters, including the “just transition” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to a low-carbon economy.
But Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop president, acknowledged there was no agreement on the draft “cover decision” text and so it had not been adopted.
“We have done our utmost; ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum ⁠such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” he said. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise ⁠that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.”
Many countries, including the EU, UK and developing countries including small island states and some of the poorest countries, said they could not support the Antalya pact deal, which was supposed to be main outcome of the Cop.
In a dramatic intervention, O’Brien said on behalf of the EU that it could not accept the final text in its current form. “It fails to meet the moment … We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” He said the EU would not accept a decision “that greenwashes fossil fuels”.
His intervention was met by applause from the hall, and was later followed by similar objections from Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway.
“This feels like a real line in the sand moment. Countries are standing up to fossil fuel interests and saying no,” said Bill Hare, the chief executive of the advisory group Climate Analytics.
But Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, who called it “the worst Cop ever”, said: “The EU has rejected this text, but it cannot wash its hands of the wreckage it helped create ... For countries facing failed harvests, destroyed homes and mounting debt, this amounts to abandonment by the wealthy nations most responsible for the crisis.
“Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves.”
Saudi Arabia defended the decision to include CCS in the text. Other countries, including the Africa group, China and Pakistan, also did not object to the deal, despite some having reservations. Pakistan told the conference that just because a few items in the pact were objectionable to some, the rest should not be sacrificed: “Climate action is not a menu from which we can select only what suits us.”
after newsletter promotion
Ghana also had criticisms of the process but did not reject the final text: “Africa has always chosen to build multilateralism rather than walk away from it.”
Close to 200 countries have been meeting in Antalya for a fortnight under the joint presidencies of Turkey and Australia, with the overrunning talks marked by long periods of deadlock as countries failed to find common ground.
The Cop co-president, Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, defended his leadership. “Australia left nothing on the field,” he said, but the red lines the presidencies had tried to negotiate were “unbridgeable”.
Asked about the consensus-based system that broke down at the talks, Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of the UN framework convention on climate change, said: “It certainly fell short today,” while emphasising that a significant number of agenda items were passed, with “real progress and concrete results”.
But for many participants, these talks exposed a failure of collective will, particularly of the rich world, to confront the urgency of the climate crisis.
While extreme weather around the world has worsened this year, claiming tens of thousands of lives in heatwaves, in disasters such as the glacier collapse in Nepal, and in droughts and floods worsened by the supercharged El Niño , the slow speed of the climate negotiations appalled even veteran participants.
“There isn’t the sense of urgency to address these issues. That to me is very frustrating,” said Mary Robinson, a former president of Ireland and former UN climate envoy, as the talks neared their scheduled close. “We have co-presidents who haven’t really been stepping up and giving that leadership.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, said: “I am deeply disappointed that Cop31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome. I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands. But this setback does not change the facts. There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science.”

articles.title_orig: Equipment outage in Atlanta causes over 1,300 Delta flight delays - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Equipment outage in Atlanta causes over 1,300 Delta flight delays - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The delays were not the result of a systems hack, Delta said.
More than 1,600 Delta Air Lines flights nationwide were delayed on Sunday due to a technical issue causing an outage to one of the airline's weight and balance systems, according to Delta.
The equipment snafu comes as millions of people prepare to travel this week for the Thanksgiving holiday, and just days after the Federal Aviation Administration issued the second nationwide ground stop since the 9/11 terrorist attacks due to an equipment installation problem that caused telecommunications issues.
"These delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems," the FAA said on Sunday about Delta's flight delays.
Delta said later Sunday afternoon that the weight and balance systems had returned to normal operation, and that the outage was not the result of a computer hack.
"Delta is rebooking customers to the next best itinerary and providing meals and hotel rooms where necessary," the airline said. "For customers facing a canceled flight and don’t wish to travel, refunds are being given."
Some 49% of all Delta flights Sunday were delayed by more than 15 minutes, Delta said, after the airline experienced an outage in a system used to calculate the weight and balance of departing flights, Delta said.
The majority of the delayed flights were at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, but the equipment issue also affected flights to Atlanta from other airports, Delta said.
"Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation. We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism," Delta said in a statement earlier Sunday.

articles.title_orig: Court bans China’s BYD from selling ‘Defender clone’ SUV in EU
articles.title_zh: Court bans China’s BYD from selling ‘Defender clone’ SUV in EU
articles.content_orig:
Reactions to ICJ ruling underline global divisions over court with China raising concerns about judicial overreach
The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.
Reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel .
The EU hailed a “landmark” judgment from the ICJ, while the UK reaffirmed “full support” for the court and the international legal order. Australia called on Myanmar to comply fully with the judgment and its obligations under international law.
But China, which has offered rare international support for Myanmar’s military rulers since they seized power five years ago, highlighted “issues such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation”.
“China … believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told a news briefing when asked about the ICJ ruling. “The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue.”
Western nations cut ties with the unstable and poor south-east Asian country after the 2021 coup that ousted a civilian-led government.
Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson said on Friday that the ruling was “unfair”, noting the judges’ nine to six vote. The country’s military rulers have denied carrying out a genocide, claiming their actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted insurgent attacks.
“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” said Khaing Khaing Soe, speaking at a press conference in the capital, Naypyidaw. “So this was not a unanimous decision … I would say it is not fair.”
The US state department said on Thursday that Washington was examining the judgment, while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.
Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), but has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.
The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”, noting that the US was the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.
In Brussels, the EU said Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.
“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson said in a statement .
“The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”.
The UK expelled Myanmar’s defence attache and called for measures to “ensure the court’s ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity”.
The ruling caps a lengthy legal campaign since August 2017 when Myanmar’s military launched what it called a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. Reports rapidly emerged of mass rapes and killings by security forces, as well as the burning of thousands of homes.
Judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.
The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the ICC – which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states – on allegations of crimes against humanity.
The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited .
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.
About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across the Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia . Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

articles.title_orig: Stocks are 'on fire sale' as Anthropic IPO fails to calm AI trade jitters
articles.title_zh: Stocks are 'on fire sale' as Anthropic IPO fails to calm AI trade jitters
articles.content_orig:
So much for buying the dip. As the S&P 500 entered correction territory and the Nasdaq-100 flirted with bear-market territory, down 19% from highs as of midday Friday, the single biggest options trade of the day was a near $100-million bet that the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) has a long way more to fall. Around 12:30 E.T., someone spent $93 million buying 20,000 380-strike puts expiring Sep. 17, 2027, according to trading data reviewed by SpotGamma and Volland, options-analytics platforms that both show the trade as a likely opening position, with volume exceeding existing open interest in the contract. The trade bets that the index will fall below $380, a nearly 8% decline from its current level. The SMH is off 40% from its recent all-time highs.
"That trade stands out big-time," wrote Jason DeLorenzo, founder and owner of Volland. "It is either a hedge or speculative, but either way it isn't a vote of confidence." The puts were bought for $46.50 a piece, an arguably expensive choice for a downside bet with volatility in the ETF trading at 70.
"You're paying a metric ton of Vega for that thing," added SpotGamma's Brent Kochuba, referring to the contract's sensitivity to changes in volatility of the underlying chip ETF. "Maybe they were a forced buyer, or maybe they're actually selling this, which can still be the case even though the price shows it happening closer to the ask."
The semiconductor index headed for a 9% drop this week alone.

articles.title_orig: Employees at Eric Trump-backed robot startup lose health benefits as company's cash crunch deepens
articles.title_zh: Employees at Eric Trump-backed robot startup lose health benefits as company's cash crunch deepens
articles.content_orig:
Employees at Foundation Future Industries were told that their health benefits through administrator Rippling have been terminated, according to a memo obtained by CNBC, adding to mounting signs of financial distress at the humanoid robot startup advised and backed by Eric Trump .
Foundation told staff in a Friday evening email that they'd be offered coverage through COBRA, the federal law that generally lets workers temporarily keep their health insurance after losing benefits by paying the full premium out of pocket.
"Because our last pay run through Rippling was in October, they have ended our benefits with them retroactive to October," a Foundation human resources manager said in the memo. "COBRA will be offered to all employees to cover November."
Foundation has garnered headlines for the bold claims that co-founder Sankaet Pathak — whose previous startup collapsed in 2024 — has made about his robots and their potential use in war zones. Employees were last paid on Oct. 15, and some inside the company are angry at Pathak for a $4.6 million loan he took from his company last year, CNBC reported earlier this month .
A Foundation spokesman didn't immediately respond to an email or phone call seeking comment.
In the staff memo, Foundation blamed Rippling for the disruption to health coverage. The startup also said it would reimburse COBRA premiums paid by workers and that it was onboarding a new benefits provider.
But employees, especially those whose family members are undergoing treatment for medical ailments, worry the company won't have funds to reimburse workers or reinstate coverage, people with direct knowledge of the situation said.
In a statement to CNBC, Rippling indicated it was Foundation's failure to pay for its employee benefits that led to the change: "If a client enrolled in Rippling's [Professional Employer Organization] is unable to meet their payroll and benefits obligations for multiple months, they will first receive a warning and if not met, they are terminated."
Foundation has been seeking a bridge loan to repay employees after its financial woes began in August. It has been in talks with three or four venture capital firms, including existing investor Tribe Capital, Pathak has told employees, according to people familiar with the situation, who asked to remain unnamed because they were not authorized to speak publicly and feared retaliation. Tribe didn't immediately return a request for comment.
The bridge loan would help the company survive until a possible $150 million investment from South Korean conglomerate Base Group lands as early as December or January, Pathak has told employees, the people said.
Base confirmed to Reuters in recent days that it was considering an investment, but the funding has not been finalized.
The potential investment would deepen business ties between the Trump family and the South Korean conglomerate, an aluminum producer also known for real estate and hospitality projects.
Base paid the Trump Organization $2 million in 2025, according to a New York Times article, drawing scrutiny from Democratic senators over conflict-of-interest concerns. Base has also pursued other business relationships with the Trump Organization, including a Trump-branded golf course in South Korea.
Eric Trump, who has invested in Foundation and was given the title of chief strategy advisor, didn't immediately respond to a CNBC email seeking comment.
The prospect of employees having to pay for their own health coverage comes as many are already drawing down savings to cover living expenses. With another scheduled payday approaching on Nov. 30, workers are facing a third straight pay cycle without income.
Many are actively interviewing for other jobs, and attendance at the company's San Francisco headquarters has fallen sharply, according to people familiar.
Frustration has boiled over into distrust of Pathak's leadership for some employees, while others hope Pathak can secure funding to repay workers and bring the company back to financial health. In conversations and memos, Pathak says that he is highly invested in securing Foundation's future, the people said.
Despite the firm's shaky finances, Foundation continued to hire for open roles until recently and some new workers have never been fully paid, said the people.
To keep employees from leaving before a possible Base Group investment, Pathak has floated the idea of offering workers equity in the startup, the people said.
At the same time, human resources staff have warned workers against taking legal action with California to recover their wages, saying that any employees who file complaints with the state would be dismissed, the people said.
Following a Nov. 14 CNBC report detailing the missed payrolls and a $4.6 million loan Pathak took from the startup in 2025, the chief executive addressed the issue in an all-hands meeting, according to the people.
Pathak defended the arrangement by telling workers that he had plowed his own money into the startup and takes only a nominal salary, the people said.
The co-founder also told employees who were in dire financial straits to contact human resources for help covering personal bills, the people added.
"I'm burning through savings just to afford my apartment," one employee told CNBC. "It's extremely unfortunate we're in this situation."

articles.title_orig: U.N. Climate Talks Collapse in a Bitter Clash Over Fossil Fuels
articles.title_zh: U.N. Climate Talks Collapse in a Bitter Clash Over Fossil Fuels
articles.content_orig:
Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’
Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.
Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.
The mandate asked countries “to elaborate by consensus”, an instrument that may not carry any legal obligations.
Although Russia led the objections using obstructive stalling tactics, other military powers invested in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other autonomous weapons.
Some argued that international humanitarian law was sufficient. More than 100 states had been pushing for a new law, saying the weapons raised entirely new challenges. European and Nato states, including Ukraine, China and Iran, expressed support or willingness for a new protocol.
The US said the need for human control over autonomous weapons had been discussed at the Apec summit in meetings between president Xi Jinping and Donald Trump this week, but the US was reluctant to agree a binding treaty.
South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany were among the defence tech powers exploring AI-enabled weapons who also expressed resistance to being bound by a new law, instead advocating for a nonbinding agreement.
The CCW is a UN forum that operates via consensus, meaning all 128 parties to the convention have to agree unanimously to pass a statement. The high threshold has resulted in the CCW failing to pass any new laws regulating weapons in the past 30 years and states seeking pathways elsewhere to pass treaties, such as the 2008 ban on cluster munitions.
The Future of Life Institute’s chair, Max Tegmark, said world leaders had failed to meet the moment this week. “Slaughterbots are already here,” he said. “Yet states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about this for the 14th year.”
Diplomats inside the negotiations said Russia had been deliberately filibustering and not working in good faith, as opposed to the US delegates, who had been seeking a path to reach a consensus statement.
The exclusion of several nonmember countries from negotiations also prompted a rare protest in the chamber on the final day of the conference, with the Egyptian delegation shouting at the conference chair.
after newsletter promotion
Israel and the US have also used AI-enabled targeting systems to conduct tens of thousands of strikes in Gaza and Iran, which have resulted in mass casualties. The Pentagon struck more than 1,000 targets in Iran on the first day of the war, and according to investigative media reports, the US military is aiming to carry out 1,000 AI-assisted targeting decisions per hour.
Critics said this outcome was a missed opportunity, noting that states had been discussing the issue of autonomous weapons, their dangers, and the need for international rules on how to restrict and regulate them for 13 years and large substantive parts of a treaty had already been settled upon.
One European diplomat said: “There was no political will to really regulate these weapons. No will commensurate to the urgency and need.”
A Human Rights Watch’s senior arms adviser, Bonnie Docherty, who had been directly involved in previously successful treaties banning cluster munitions and nuclear weapons, said autonomous weapons needed binding law. She noted that treaties could be negotiated within 15 months and dismissed the US’s proposal of five years to sort out a mandate.
A bloc of seven countries – Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama – had led the push for a binding treaty to be negotiated within one year.
On Wednesday Brazil’s delegate told the floor: “These are not weapons of the future being discussed here, these are already in use and being further developed. We are late in developing these norms and rules to regulate these lethal autonomous weapons systems.”

articles.title_orig: COP31 climate talks fail to reach deal amid fossil fuel and money rows
articles.title_zh: COP31 climate talks fail to reach deal amid fossil fuel and money rows
articles.content_orig:
Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.
Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.
But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.
Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.
The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.
UN secretary general Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".
He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".
After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday morning to try to break the deadlock.
But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023 , when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.
The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change".
"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.
Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.
A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.
Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions.
Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".
Whatâs next after no deal at COP31 climate talks?
Another major sticking point has been money for poorer countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, such as more intense heatwaves and more severe droughts.
Last year at COP30 in Brazil , nations agreed to triple the finance for that purpose.
But this year's deal contained no reference to concrete figures, nor the baseline against which that pledge would be measured. This raised fears it would give richer nations too much wriggle room.
"Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed," said Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, an African climate and energy think tank.
The UK's Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, described the failure to reach a political agreement as "immensely disappointing".
"This only strengthens our resolve to work with partners around the world on the genuine progress made in Antalya on tackling the climate crisis," she said, adding that the UK's commitment was "unwavering".
While talks were hosted in Antalya in Turkey, Australia led the official negotiations - creating what some observers described as a chaotic dynamic.
Chris Bowen, Australian government minister and COP31 president of negotiations, said that there were "unbridgeable red lines" in the discussions.
He pointed to "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". At the same time, "the impacts of climate change are getting worse", he said, raising the stakes.
The year 2026 could end as the hottest on record and has brought extreme weather and natural hazards to much of the world, from summer heat and drought in Europe to flash flooding in Nepal .
And COP31 was the first annual UN conference to formally discuss how one of the key international targets for limiting climate change would be missed.
In the Paris talks of 2015 , nearly 200 countries agreed to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels of the late 1800s, aimed at avoiding some of the worst effects of climate change.
The UN says that the Paris deal has driven "near-universal" climate action. In the early 2010s, global warming of 4C or more was thought to be a serious possibility by the end of the century.
Now, the world is likely to limit warming to about 2.8C by 2100 based on current government policies, the UN says.
But action has not been fast enough to meet that Paris goal, with the world likely to "overshoot" 1.5C of long-term warming in the next few years.
Many countries say they are committed to eventually bringing warming back down to 1.5C, but that will require an ambitious ramping up of technologies - which do not yet exist at scale - to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
Although the main deal fell through, some agreements were reached, including progress on a "just transition mechanism" - a framework to support workers and communities as economies shift towards clean energy.
The COP31 president also said that more than 80 countries backed Turkey's target to increase the share of global energy use met by electricity to 35% by 2035
But following today's events, some have questioned whether the UN climate process - which relies on consensus - can succeed in a geopolitically divided world.
The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the process, with the next conference scheduled for November 2027, COP32 in Ethiopia.
"[The consensus process] has worked to get us where we are," he told the BBC. "It got us through Paris... so it can work," but acknowledged it "fell short" today.
The UN climate process has "suffered setback before and come back stronger," Stiell told delegates. "It must do so again."

articles.title_orig: Tanker incident “involving military forces” reported in Hormuz
articles.title_zh: Tanker incident “involving military forces” reported in Hormuz
articles.content_orig:
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) announced on Sunday evening that “a tanker was involved in an incident with military forces in the Gulf of Oman,” east of the Strait of Hormuz, near the southern Iranian city of Charbahar.
The UKMTO wording identifying “military forces” may indicate a US military action against a tanker, while the reported location is close to the US navy blockade line.
Also, the location and the timing of the incident are consistent of where an Iranian tanker would be in its attempt to break the US military naval blockade had it sailed from Kharg Island on Sunday morning.
“A company security officer alerted UKMTO to the incident. Authorities are aware and investigations are ongoing,” the UKMTO bulletin also said.
Iran had threatened for several days that any attempt by the US military to stop the Iranian tankers would result in a “fierce military response” and immediate Iranian strikes on energy infrastructures across the Gulf.
Earlier on Sunday, Iranian media quoting Iran’s navy said two supertankers caught fire after hitting mines in a “restricted area” east of the Strait of Hormuz and north of Ghanam Island. It was unclear if the two incidents were connected.
On Saturday, Iran’s deputy minister of foreign affairs Kazem Gharibabadi told Iranian media that the US blockade of Iranian ports “is an act of war and we will take any necessary measures to break this economic siege,” amid reports that as more than 14 Iranian tankers were being prepared off Kharg Island to break out of the US military blockade.
Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian also said that Iran is subject to a “silent economic war” which is “tougher than a war with missiles,” adding that Iran has the capability to withstand it.

S o, did you invest in the market-leading company that has warned its technology could ultimately help destroy humanity?
You could have put a gun to my head and I still wouldn’t have signed up for shares in Anthropic , the artificial intelligence giant behind AI assistant Claude, that warned artificial intelligence could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" in documents accompanying its blockbuster stock market flotation .
To me, it felt a bit like Sarah Connor, heroine of the Terminator films, opening the financial pages to discover that Skynet is floating on Wall Street. Our robots might wipe out humanity… but they make awesome work colleagues!
But if you signed up, you may be disappointed with your allocation.
The shares were in demand among big boys at moneybags institutions. Even a company the size of Anthropic, with the degree of control held by the founders (the big seven newly minted multi-billionaires have 50.1 per cent under its somewhat controversial governance structure), has to keep them sweet.
The small fry - so you and me - could apply for as little as £250 via Hargreaves Lansdown and other platforms. Even if you get only a limited number, this democratisation of the stock market is a welcome development. Why should the big institutions have all the fun? But just because you can buy something doesn't mean you should.
We’re about to find out whether the market’s recent bout of AI nervousness holds true. The reported institutional demand is encouraging for the company. But will that remain the case over the next few days, once the shares start trading and find a level?
I confess Anthropic had already put me off, with its relentlessly irritating podcast advertising. One featured breathless workers discussing their awesome new colleague, Claude , as though he were the office heartthrob. But my reservations go considerably deeper than its marketing department.
It is undeniably a remarkable business. Its annualised revenue reportedly reached $81bn in October. That's phenomenal growth for a company founded just five years ago.
Unfortunately, the numbers on the other side of the ledger are equally extraordinary. Anthropic has computing commitments approaching $900bn. Building the AI revolution requires astonishing quantities of expensive infrastructure, energy and processing power.
And nobody can confidently predict how much profit all this spending will ultimately generate.
That's the problem with a trillion-dollar valuation. Investors aren't simply betting that AI will transform the world. They're betting that Anthropic will capture enough of that transformation to justify its enormous price tag. Those are two very different propositions.
There's another intriguing wrinkle. Some critics suspect the AI giants’ enthusiasm for warnings about existential risk also serves their commercial interests.
Regulation can be a wonderful thing when you're already established. Compliance is expensive. Smaller competitors, perhaps a few Stanford dropouts working on the next technological revolution in an outrageously overpriced San Francisco bedsit, might struggle to afford it.
That doesn't mean Anthropic's safety concerns are insincere. But regulation that protects humanity could also protect the industry's incumbents from competition.
And competition, rather than Claude listening to Guns N' Roses' Appetite for Destruction and getting ideas, may prove the more immediate threat to shareholders.
An investment professional I spoke to wouldn't touch these valuations . The concern isn't whether AI has a future; of course it does. It's whether investors are paying so much for that future that even spectacular success might disappoint them.
Remember: technology changes quickly. Today's cuddly, indispensable AI assistant could become tomorrow's obsolete software . In five years, Anthropic's business might look unrecognisable. Or it may just find itself struggling to keep up.
That’s the risk taken by those who took a punt. They might make a fortune. They should do okay if Anthropic emerges as one of the AI winners. But even that’s a big if.
No one should confuse buying into the future with buying a good investment. Remember: even if Anthropic’s AI bots don't destroy humanity, there's nothing stopping them from destroying your savings. Here endeth the lesson. Now let’s sit back and watch that share price. Good luck!

articles.title_orig: Forget the mortgage. Behold the hidden costs of homeownership
articles.title_zh: Forget the mortgage. Behold the hidden costs of homeownership
articles.content_orig:
Owning residential property in the United States costs considerably more than making mortgage payments, with homeowners spending an average of $21,466 annually on additional expenses, according to an Insurify analysis published November 22, 2026. Maintenance, utilities, property taxes, and insurance account for 25.6% of the median household's annual income, while five states exceed $30,000 in yearly non-mortgage costs.
The nationwide figure represents a 2% increase from the previous year. The expenses also affect homeowners who have completely paid off their mortgages, while US Census Bureau data cited by Newsweek shows that 59% of homeowners still make mortgage payments.
Maintenance represents the largest expense, averaging $7,374 annually. Utilities contribute another $5,649, while property taxes account for $4,427, according to Insurify.
California leads the national ranking with $35,527 in annual non-mortgage ownership expenses. Hawaii follows at $35,269, while Massachusetts reaches $33,281. New Jersey records $31,556 and Connecticut $30,069, placing all five states above the $30,000 threshold.
California homeowners experienced a 4% increase in overall additional expenses, equivalent to $1,466 annually. Utility costs climbed 16%, while home insurance expenses increased 8% as state regulators worked to stabilize the insurance market and prevent private insurers from withdrawing from vulnerable areas amid increasingly frequent and severe extreme weather.
Hawaii recorded a 2% increase, adding $530 to annual expenses. Massachusetts was the only state among the five most expensive markets to register a decline, with costs falling 1%, or $378. New Jersey experienced a 4% increase of $1,132, while Connecticut recorded a 1% rise of $292.
New York came close to joining the five most expensive states, with annual non-mortgage expenses reaching $29,359. The figure represented a 3% increase, equivalent to $722, compared with the previous year.
At the lower end of the ranking, West Virginia recorded the country's lowest annual non-mortgage ownership expenses at $13,462. Arkansas followed with $14,445, Mississippi with $14,862, Kentucky with $15,086, and Indiana with $15,571. Insurify found that 33 states had expenses below the national average.
Despite their comparatively affordable ownership costs, West Virginia, South Carolina, and Minnesota experienced annual increases of approximately 9%. Insurance premiums contributed significantly to the increases in South Carolina and Minnesota.
Annual home insurance costs in South Carolina surged 41% to $3,264. Minnesota experienced an even larger percentage increase of 56%, bringing its average annual premium to $3,987. Florida continued to have the highest average homeowners insurance bill nationwide at $8,486 annually.
Flood coverage presents another financial challenge. The average annual cost of insurance through the National Flood Insurance Program increased 9%, according to the analysis. Standard homeowners insurance policies generally exclude flood damage, while the federal program provides most flood insurance policies nationwide.
Housing affordability concerns also extend to younger generations. An Insurify survey found that 24% of Generation Z respondents believed purchasing a home would always remain financially out of reach.
Among Generation Z homeowners between ages 22 and 28, nearly 90% acknowledged underestimating certain expenses associated with owning property. The findings highlight the additional financial responsibilities that prospective buyers may encounter beyond their mortgage payments.
Mallory Mooney, director of sales and service at Insurify, emphasized the importance of accounting for recurring ownership expenses before purchasing a property.
" Homeownership has its perks, but buying a home without budgeting for additional upkeep costs — property taxes, home insurance, and others — can lead to regrets down the line," said Mallory Mooney, director of sales and service at Insurify.

It runs off, the buck gives chase, and at least as far as the matter is concerned in this footage, the doe is safe.

The little pump fake by the bobcat didn't fool the buck at all. This wasn’t going to be a playful exchange.
The buck saw the move from a mile away and charged immediately. The bobcat should have known better once the buck headed its way.
Perhaps it fell for the claim that chivalry was dead and thought it could chase the buck off and force it to leave his lady unprotected. That was not the case.
Sean Joseph is a writer for OutKick.

articles.title_orig: Lebanese villagers return to wrecked homes as the Israeli army pulls back
articles.title_zh: Lebanese villagers return to wrecked homes as the Israeli army pulls back
articles.content_orig:
A destroyed home in the village of Zawtar al-Gharbiyah in southern Lebanon. The family says Israeli forces demolished their home and two other homes of extended family when they occupied the village after a U.S.-brokered ceasefire. Mohammed Yassine for NPR hide caption
ZAWTAR AL-GHARBIYAH, Lebanon — After two decades of working installing vehicle air conditioning in Saudi Arabia, Atef Kadouh saved up enough money to build a house in his hometown in southern Lebanon.
He and his wife, Soumaya Yaghi lived in the house for 40 years and had five children — all born at home.
A photo of the youngest, Adel, is propped up in a basket of dried flowers near the doorway.
Adel, clean-cut with a trimmed beard, was a sports teacher and a basketball champion who was planning to travel to France this summer to pursue his doctorate. When the war with Israel began this year, he decided to volunteer as an ambulance driver.
Soumaya Yaghi stands in her damaged home. Israeli forces occupied the house while they were in the village and it was set on fire as they left. The second floor was burned almost completely. Mohammed Yassine for NPR hide caption
The Israeli military killed him and four other medics on March 28 in a drone strike as the first responders buried a 75-year-old man who had died in hospital.
"This one broke me," his father says. "He was my youngest son, 27 years old. There have been wars in every country in the world but there are rules for war … you attack a paramedic rescuing wounded people, children? He was not a fighter at the front."
Soumaya Yaghi holds an image of her son Adel, a volunteer ambulance driver who was killed in an Israeli airstrike in March along with four other paramedics as they were burying an elderly man who had died in hospital. Mohammed Yassine for NPR hide caption
He says he warned his son that Israel could not be trusted not to kill medical personnel.
"He would not listen to me. He said, 'Dad there are wounded children — we have to go rescue them,'" he says.
Lebanon's Health Ministry says Israel has killed more than 135 first responders and medical staff in the past two years.
Asked about this airstrike, the Israeli military replied, without providing proof, that militants routinely pose as paramedics and transport weapons in ambulances for the militant group Hezbollah and its allies.
It did not respond to follow-up questions pointing out the five were not killed in an ambulance but at a burial.
A family goes through the rubble of their home after it was demolished by Israeli forces when they occupied the village. They have brought in a bulldozer to clear the rubble. Mohammed Yassine for NPR hide caption
The Kadouh family returned to the village in July when it became the first and until now only test of a U.S.-brokered plan for Israeli forces to withdraw and the Lebanese army to take over.
The plan is aimed at keeping Iran-backed Hezbollah out of the area, after they started firing rockets across the nearby border in solidarity with the Palestinian militant group Hamas who launched a surprise attack on southern Israel in October 2023.
Packaging in Hebrew left behind after Israeli soldiers occupied the Kadouhs' home before the house was set on fire as Israeli forces withdrew. Mohammed Yassine for NPR hide caption
Israel responded with devastating air strikes and eventually a ground invasion, and says it has continued attacks in south Lebanon following a U.S.-brokered ceasefire this year to eliminate what it believes are continued threats to northern Israel. Israel's defense minister has acknowledged destroying more than 20,000 homes across the Lebanese border in a self-declared security zone.
When Kadouh and Yaghi returned to the village, they found that Israeli soldiers had occupied their house. And then it had been set on fire.
Atef Kadouh sits in the middle of his burned and damaged house in south Lebanon after Israeli forces occupied the house and then withdrew in a plan to hand over security to Lebanese forces. Mohammed Yassine for NPR hide caption
Upstairs in the hallway, near scorched walls and shattered windows, what appeared to be a work roster was written on the wall in blue marker in Hebrew with the first names of Israeli soldiers.
Almost everything in the house had been destroyed. Appliances — the fridge, freezer and washing machine — had bullet holes in them. Some, along with furniture, had been pushed over the second floor balcony, smashing on the ground below.
Kadouh says they knew from satellite photos there was destruction in their village "but the level of destruction — we were not expecting that. Everything that could be broken they broke."
In the kitchen were shattered floor tiles and kitchen cupboards wrenched from the walls.
The fire appeared to be set as the soldiers were leaving. Blackened, burned food packets — fruit boxes and cans of energy drinks with Hebrew writing — were on the floor along with rotting sandwiches.
In their 18-month-old grandson's bedroom, soot from a scorched ceiling dripped down on walls decorated with images of hot-air balloons and teddy bears climbing ladders to the moon.
Yaghi shows a bullet — one of many she says she found throughout the house. The spent engine casing of a missile or a drone with English markings reading "propulsion unit – tactical" was found in one of the rooms.
Soumaya Yaghi holds the metal casing of a drone or missile with English-language markings found in their home along with bullets throughout the house. Mohammed Yassine for NPR hide caption
There is no running water or electricity — Kadouh says the Israeli military destroyed the solar panels.
The Lebanese army told them that when it reentered the village many of the houses had been rigged to be blown up. It said it dismantled explosives left by Israeli forces in their house and others.
A man walks through the rubble of his destroyed home in Zawtar al-Gharbiyah, Lebanon. Mohammed Yassine for NPR hide caption
The Israeli army did not reply to NPR queries about why the house was damaged or set on fire. It said military policy bars burning homes or leaving explosives.
Unable to enter the village while Israeli forces were there, Kadouh said he saw a tank in their courtyard from drone images posted on social media.
Smoke rises from an Israeli attack in the village of Kfar Tebnit, Lebanon. Mohammed Yassine for NPR hide caption
Yaghi says the Israeli army used a bulldozer to uproot the trees — including the pine trees which yield one of their most prized cash crops: pine nuts. When they had killed the trees, she says they demolished the family's garage and destroyed their tractor.
"We are back to square one," Kadouh says. "Starting from scratch."
Even more precarious, though, than when they started decades ago. Despite a ceasefire, smoke rises from a nearby village where Israel is still attacking.
Amid all the damage, the destruction of the family's trees cuts the deepest.
"I tended to them as if they were small children — they were all dear to me," Kadouh says.
Yaghi points out where there were fruit-bearing cactus, olive trees, a fig tree one of her sons brought from Italy, avocado trees and fields of thyme, avocado.
Up until a decade ago, almost everyone here grew tobacco, diversifying crops when that market collapsed.
"We raised our children through hard work and thank God all of them were educated," Yaghi says, noting with pride that they all became professionals.
She maintains a visceral connection to the land.
"Record this," she asks, walking next to rose bushes that have begun to bloom again. "Our land is a paradise with everything in it. Our life is this land. Our life is our homes. Even if we were to die in our homes it would be much better than to live outside."
A man walks past a damaged mosque in the village of Zawtar al-Gharbiyah, Lebanon. There was still no electricity or running water in the village after attacks on the infrastructure. Mohammed Yassine for NPR hide caption
Villagers here feel aban

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Stock Has A Cockroach Problem. What Comes Next Could Be Worse
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Stock Has A Cockroach Problem. What Comes Next Could Be Worse
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia’s leadership sought to set a path forward on Tuesday’s earnings call in the wake of former CEO Jensen Huang’s departure — defying calls to re-hire him, reassuring investors that demand for Nvidia’s products remains strong, and indicating that the leadership shakeup could prompt a new or more cautious approach to key elements of the company’s business.
The company has been rocked by scandal, national security concerns and the resignation of Huang, its founder and CEO of 33 years. And leadership was under pressure to reassure nervous investors Tuesday evening, with Nvidia having lost $751 billion in market value since last Sunday.
Many lingering questions remain. But investors appeared at least somewhat mollified by the comments and earnings results: shares ticked up nearly 5% in after-hours trading following the call.
Nvidia rules out Jensen Huang’s return as CEO, tells investors ‘we’ve got this’
Nvidia Board Chair Harvey Jones kicked off the earnings call by saying the board does not intend to reinstate Huang as CEO, despite Huang’s statement earlier Tuesday that he would be “honored” to return should the board allow it.
Jones said the board has “every confidence” in CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress to lead the company as it searches for a permanent replacement. He added the board wants to install a permanent CEO “as quickly as possible,” but it wouldn’t rush to appoint someone until it finds “exactly the right person.”
The board is considering internal and external candidates for the role. And while Jones offered no further hints on who is under consideration, Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president and general manager of Hyperscale and High-Performance Computing, joined Kress to take analyst questions on the call — a signal of his importance as a senior leader at the company.
Jones indicated that the board is taking the national security concerns into consideration in its search.
“The board appreciates that we’re living in a world where the advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are making major changes in our marketplace,” Jones said. “Our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully.”
Why crisis at NVIDIA reverberates across the AI industry
Nvidia has played a key role in fueling the growth of the AI ecosystem by providing financing and investment to its customers to purchase its chips and build AI infrastructure.
Some industry analysts have questioned whether that will continue without Huang, who was considered the industry’s master dealmaker, even as others criticized the practice as “circular financing” that has artificially inflated the market.
Kress said on the call that the company has committed more than $100 billion to such deals as of the end of the quarter ended in October. However, she indicated that the company will carefully evaluate any deals to back would-be customers going forward.
“We remain thoughtful in how we participate and disciplined in how we commit capital,” Kress said. “We are proud of the role that we have played so far in supporting the ecosystem. As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.”
Beyond its existing deals, Nvidia will take “a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing,” she said.
The company earned $2.4 billion in sales of licensed chips to China during the third quarter — comprising just over 2% of the total revenue in its core data center business unit. But the company has ceased shipments to the country, Kress said during Tuesday’s call.
That news comes as the company faces increased scrutiny from US officials over the potential illicit transfer of its chips to China.
How the Nvidia scandal lifted the curtain on a loophole that’s giving China access to US chips
A complex network of loopholes of shell corporations and unauthorized brokers, often operating via countries like Singapore, are believed to have enabled the transfer of millions of Nvidia chips to China in violation of export controls. Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., estimated that China and Hong Kong “could comprise roughly 15%” of Nvidia’s previous revenues “when considering potential loopholes throughout Asia.”
The Commerce Department on Monday announced tighter export restrictions to prevent China from accessing sensitive, AI-powering computer chips via data centers in third-party countries.
The company is assuming no revenue from sales of licensed chips to China in the fourth quarter.
Even prior to Huang’s exit, questions were swirling about whether major tech companies might pull back on their spending on AI infrastructure as they face scrutiny from investors over when the technology will produce meaningful returns.
But Kress said demand for Nvidia’s products continues to outstrip supply, especially as a growing slate of companies and consumers seek to implement computing-intensive AI agents .
“Even in the last week, the continued ask is: How are we going to receive more and more supply to help (customers) with the demand that they have in front of them,” Kress said.
That growing demand pushed the company’s projection for full-year revenue growth in 2028 to 75%, up from its earlier projection of 70%. Nvidia also reported better-than-expected guidance for sales in the final quarter of this year.
“We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners,” following Huang’s resignation, Kress said. “They’re all 100% behind us.”

articles.title_orig: Ferrari's New 296 Challenge Stradale Is A 670-HP Race Car You Can Drive Home
articles.title_zh: Ferrari's New 296 Challenge Stradale Is A 670-HP Race Car You Can Drive Home
articles.content_orig:
The curtains open, and for a moment, you're completely transfixed. You know right away that you're looking at something special. This car represents a turning point for Ferrari, a significant departure from what came before. It's a genuine race car that's still somehow legal to drive on the street.
"This is a disruption of balance," says one of the people most closely involved in bringing the car to life. It's easy to see what he means. Even standing still, the Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale looks like a car built with one thing in mind: setting lap times.
Ferrari even calls it "the production car with the closest connection to a competition vehicle."
No hybrid system. 670 horsepower. Just 2,932 pounds. And 1,360 pounds of downforce at 155 miles per hour. The car was developed alongside the 296 Challenge Evo , which will compete in Ferrari's one-make racing series starting in 2027. The price? Around $307,000.
Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale
"It's a physical car, fundamentally different to drive. It's not like the 296 Speciale , which is easier and more immediate." Those two sentences tell you almost everything you need to know.
The Speciale is incredibly fast, but it's also approachable. Its electric motor helps with corner exits, drifting, and straight-line acceleration. The Challenge Stradale does away with all of that. There's no hybrid system and no electric motor to fill in the gaps. It's a raw, uncompromising machine with a narrower margin for error, one that relies on aerodynamics to do much of the heavy lifting.
The connection between Ferrari's road cars and its racing program goes back to the company's roots. Enzo Ferrari lived for competition, and in the early days, building road cars was largely a way to fund his racing ambitions. That relationship continues today through the Ferrari Challenge, a customer racing series that has been running since 1993.
It started with the 348, followed by the F355, 360, and every generation since. The 296 Challenge Stradale brings that racing DNA closer to the road than any production Ferrari before it.
Under the hood is the familiar twin-turbocharged 3.0-liter V6 from the 296, with both turbochargers mounted inside the V. The difference is that it now works entirely on its own, producing:
For comparison, the competition-focused 296 Challenge Evo produces 700 hp.
The turbochargers are carried over from the 296 Challenge, as are the thermal barriers. Ferrari focused its development work on boost pressure, variable valve timing, and insulation. The result is a dynamic torque increase of more than 32 percent compared to the 296 GTB. Without an electric motor smoothing things out, throttle response is also much sharper.
The eight-speed dual-clutch transmission has two distinct personalities. Push the car hard, and it switches to the aggressive shifting logic from the 296 Challenge, delivering gear changes in around 170 milliseconds. At lower speeds, it adopts a smoother calibration borrowed from the SF90 XX Stradale. The exhaust note builds all the way to 8,500 rpm, exiting through twin tailpipes derived from the race car.
Performance is predictably serious. The 296 Challenge Stradale hits 60 mph in 2.8 seconds, reaches 124 mph in 7.9 seconds, and tops out at more than 186 mph. Around Ferrari's Fiorano test track, it completes a lap in 1 minute and 18.5 seconds.
The dry weight is just 2,932 pounds with optional equipment, making it 308 pounds lighter than the 296 GTB. That's also the same figure as the 296 Challenge Evo. The result is a power-to-weight ratio of 4.37 pounds per horsepower.
A big part of the weight savings comes from removing the battery and electric motor. Ferrari also fitted a dedicated transmission with a lighter shaft and casing. Then there's the carbon fiber, which appears throughout the car:
For the first time on a production Ferrari, buyers can also request removable seat coverings, leaving parts of the underlying structure exposed.
One figure says a lot about how the Challenge Stradale behaves through corners: body roll is down 68 percent compared to the 296 GTB. Lateral performance improves by 7 percent, while stability increases by 34 percent.
The springs are roughly twice as stiff, requiring an additional spring mounted in series with the main one. It's a setup borrowed directly from the 296 Challenge Evo. The semi-active dampers also get two additional rebound settings, allowing Ferrari to retain at least some compliance when driving on public roads.
The car rides on Pirelli P Zero R tires, with semi-slick P Zero Trofeo RS tires available as an option. Both were specifically developed for the car.
With no regenerative braking system to rely on, stopping power comes entirely from the carbon-ceramic brakes. The front discs measure 15.7 x 1.5 inches, while the rear ones measure 15 x 1.3 inches. Ferrari says the car can stop from 124 mph in just 331 feet.
The traction control system is predictive and calibrated specifically for track driving, marking a first for a road-going Ferrari. It's all managed by the FIVE system, derived from the one used in the F80.
The headline aerodynamic figure is 1,360 pounds of downforce at 155 mph, a 72 percent increase over the 296 GTB. Ferrari achieves this through several carefully designed elements:
At the rear, a fixed wing derived from the 296 Challenge Evo generates 595 pounds of downforce on its own. There's one notable difference, though. Unlike the race car, the wing doesn't use a swan-neck mounting design. Instead, its supports attach from underneath to meet road homologation requirements, particularly those in the United States.
Ferrari's Centro Stile, led by Flavio Manzoni, took the clean design of the 296 and gave it a much more aggressive makeover. A technical insert on the hood, a wing suspended between two bumper-mounted "claws" inspired by the Evo, black metal mesh at the rear, and a double-keel diffuser all serve the same purpose. Here, form follows function.
Buyers looking to make their cars stand out can choose from a dedicated livery, three matte-finish wheel options, and even colored tire inserts through Pirelli's Color Edition program.
The Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale starts at approximately $307,000.

articles.title_orig: Oh No, I Can’t Stop Watching People Play ‘GTA VI’
articles.title_zh: Oh No, I Can’t Stop Watching People Play ‘GTA VI’
articles.content_orig:
12:31 PM EST on November 22, 2026
I did not imagine that the release of Grand Theft Auto VI would have any meaningful impact on my life, for the simple reason that I am not a gamer. I know and even respect a few people for whom video games are important, but I mainly regard this in the same way I do friends who really like square dancing, or go to church: nice for them, but not really my business.
And while I have, in the past, dated gamers and even come to occasionally enjoy watching them play video games, that was mainly because I'm bossy and liked telling them go over there or open that box I bet there's something inside. Backseat driving a video game can be fun but only insofar as I can manipulate what's happening. The appeal of Twitch, where you are simply one of dozens or hundreds of spectators watching someone else play a game has always been totally, utterly alien to me. This would be true even without the dangers of encountering slurs in a chat or being confronted by the ever present sight of anything that could be reasonably called "a gaming rig." No thank you.
And yet, I have found my conviction wavering recently as I find myself strangely compelled to click on clip after clip of people playing GTA VI . It started innocently enough, as people kept insisting that this game was teaching men to be thoughtful partners. I watched clips of people doing things Lucia will appreciate: buying groceries, taking her shopping, picking up flowers. I watched a guy make thoughtful decisions about how she might like to wear her hair. Soon I'd moved on to following along as people make Jason lovingly turn their house into a home , or invite Lucia to take the driver's seat on an aquatic adventure.
Before long, my attention ranged beyond the tender dynamics of this romance between down-on-their-luck criminals. I was enthralled by this one streamer pretending to host a nature documentary while wandering around the wilderness of Leonida (fake Florida.) I cheered as Jason is, for reasons that remain completely beyond me, rescued by a dog driving a jetski . I even found myself beguiled by the many ways a digitally rendered human body can react to getting hit by a basketball.
Finally, I felt something definitively crack open in my heart as I watched this man in raptures about the game's authentic depiction of a transmission tower:
Enjoy this guy getting bricked over the detail of towers in GTA6
I do not know what this means for me, and perhaps it will pass. I still have no intention of buying a console, or doing anything as unseemly as joining Twitch. But it would be dishonest to go on pretending that I am unmoved by this video game. Just look at those towers, boys. Just look at them.
