articles.title_orig: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
articles.title_zh: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
articles.content_orig:
A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.
The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard.
It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday afternoon that fire was no longer visible from the outside but thermal cameras showed that some containers on the ship were still warm.
The Sparta II was "slightly listing", Finnish authorities added, but the "situation is stable" and no fuel or other "hazardous substance leaks" had been detected.
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones appeared to have been used in the strike and that there was "no threat" to his territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
While Besprozvannykh initially said the crew of the Sparta II intended to repair the ship and carry on their journey, the Finnish Border Guard later said they had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was en route to Russia.
Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, director of maritime operations at the Finnish Border Guard, said during a news conference on Sunday that one Sparta II crew member had suffered minor injuries.
The Russian rescue vessel Murman is leading towing operations with the support of a Finnish guard ship and a Estonian naval patrol vessel.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Border Guard was responsible for the investigation into the attack and was co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland .

articles.title_orig: Transcript: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 22, 2026
articles.title_zh: Transcript: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 22, 2026
articles.content_orig:
The following is the transcript of the interview with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 22, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We begin with the Secretary of the Treasury, Scott Bessent. It's good to have you here and in person, sir.
U.S. TREASURY SECRETARY SCOTT BESSENT: Margaret, good to see you.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So there were thousands of customers across America who, when they went to some of the biggest banks, had issues this past week with tech outages, and it caused a bit of a panic with people pulling out cash. In this age of AI, what should Americans be prepared for, and should they worry about their financial institutions?
SEC. BESSENT: It's a good good question, Margaret. And no, they shouldn't. The banks have been at the forefront of cybersecurity for decades. They experience attacks every day, every week, every month, and they are by far the most resilient companies in the U.S. economy. What we are seeing as they, because of the SI, as they go into patch their security systems, the patches may cause a glitch, which is what happened last week. J.P. Morgan went in, and I think the American people should think of it as a vaccine. Your arm may hurt, you may feel a little bad the next day, but it increases your long-term immunity and resiliency.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay. Well, there's other concerns about AI, as you know, and we've seen in the stock market anxiety, a real sell-off over the past week. Nvidia is sometimes referred to as the central bank of AI, since it uses its cash to finance things like data centers and essentially boost demand for its own sales. We have a graphic there, sort of showing the gist of that. I mean, when you look at its size and how interwoven it is in the tech industry. Do you worry that this kind of circular financing means that one company is becoming so hugely important that it could have ripple effects if something goes wrong?
SEC. BESSENT: Well, look, Nvidia is one of our great companies with the management chains. The board has slowed things down. The CFO is now in charge, so you know, I believe that she understands the financing quite well. And no, as Nvidia continues to be fantastically profitable, and there is near unlimited demand for their chips worldwide.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Do you—how do you understand what happened in the markets this past week?
SEC. BESSENT: Well, I think it's a combination of things. You know, we could see that the market sell-off actually began as the Democrats moved ahead in the polls and then accelerated after Election Day. The Democratic position on the SI buildout has spooked a lot of investors in terms of slowing it down. We've also seen some very hawkish remarks from the Federal Reserve. Many people believe that they may be making a policy mistake if they over-tighten. We've seen a substantial tightening in financial conditions over the past few months. So, you know, I think it was a combination of these things.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, President Trump gave that 90-minute or so press conference on Friday, and he did talk about things in AI. Among many things, he said, take a listen to this.
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen, and we're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.
MARGARET BRENNAN: How is that policy going to work, and won't that also inhibit the sector?
SEC. BESSENT: Well, I haven't spoken to the president about that. I was sitting in that press conference, and I didn't get a chance to speak to him after that. But look, I think the president's very concerned that we don't do a big technology transfer offshore. What we've seen, that the U.S. used to be the leader in the chip industry, and now we see that 97% of the high-end chips are made in Taiwan, which creates a strategic vulnerability.
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's been the case.
SEC. BESSENT: Well, this administration is working to bring them back. There are large fabs being built by TSMC in Arizona, and we hope to have substantial onshoring of the chip business by the end of this administration. So, I think he's worried about the same thing happening with data centers.
MARGARET BRENNAN: With data centers, so one of the arguments against this, and the Wall Street Journal editorial board was pointing out a challenge here, is that if American companies can't build data centers and their AI models close to the markets they're trying to sell into, it will basically give their competitors, the Chinese, an edge.
SEC. BESSENT: Well, look, I think that the SI is very fungible. That companies access U.S. centers. There are many centers in Southeast Asia. They get access from around the world. So I think the real thing here is going to be, and I've said it many times before the election. The industry has done a terrible job of explaining themselves to the American people, and I think they need to have a conversation with the American people, with the communities where these centers are built, and rebuild public trust. And I think once we see that, then we could see a more substantial build out here in the U.S.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, so what the president announced was not reversing, for example, what the U.S. was encouraging in the United Arab Emirates with these data centers being built in some of our Gulf allies.
SEC. BESSENT: No, he's talking about American companies doing it.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, let me ask you about Nvidia in particular and what's been happening in terms of the ongoing revelations. Multiple congressional committees, federal prosecutors, and presumably regulators here in the United States are probing the role Nvidia played in sending advanced AI computer chips to China. On Fox last Sunday, I watched your interview. It was pretty extraordinary. You did not parse words. You referred to a culture of non-compliance at Nvidia. The possibility that they were quote "pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings." You said you needed answers to what was going on within 10 days. That was seven days ago. Have you gotten the answers you need?
SEC. BESSENT: We don't, Margaret. And I think the important word there is possibility. And we have seen. We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers, and we do need answers. And back to your question about the centrality of Nvidia to the SI system, it behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was. Was there promiscuous attitude toward this, and where—if it happened—where were the faults, and then they can move on.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So when you say we, you mean to Treasury? You're expecting those answers to go to Treasury, or they're expecting to go to the White House?
SEC. BESSENT: To the administration.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Because there was a lot of reporting that Nvidia's business deals were often based on handshakes. That doesn't leave a lot of a paper trail. How challenging is this for regulators to get to the bottom of what the CEO was doing? I know you said the CFO is at the helm, but last Sunday you said basically they need to clean up shop and get someone from the outside to run the place.
SEC. BESSENT: Well, what I said was we do need to see who was in charge of compliance there. Normally, it's the legal department, the general counsel's office. So we'll see what they have to say. But you know, in terms of handshake deals, for deals that size, there's no such thing as an untraceable handshake deal, there are bills blading that movement. There are money movements, so you know, they may not be the 100-page documents, but there, it will be possible to understand what has gone on here.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I mean, that's an extraordinary charge though, a culture of non-compliance.
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's not just the foibles of one man.
SEC. BESSENT:

articles.title_orig: Delta tech issue delays hundreds of flights in and out of Atlanta ahead of Thanksgiving
articles.title_zh: Delta tech issue delays hundreds of flights in and out of Atlanta ahead of Thanksgiving
articles.content_orig:
NBC NEWS PROJECTION: Democrats secure the largest House majority for either party since 1992
A problem with the system Delta Air Lines uses to calculate aircraft weight and balance delayed its flights nationwide Sunday as Thanksgiving travel got underway.
The Federal Aviation Administration lifted its ground delay program for Atlanta-bound Delta flights at 11:26 a.m. ET, but by 1:55 p.m. ET, 997 flights into and out of Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport had been delayed and 26 had been canceled, according to FlightAware.
The FAA briefly halted Atlanta-bound flights Sunday morning, then replaced the ground stop with a program that allowed flights to depart at staggered times. The delay program, requested by Delta, applied to the airline and its regional carriers flying into Hartsfield-Jackson from the contiguous United States.
The FAA had projected delays of 57 minutes on average and lasting up to 1 hour and 51 minutes.
Delta said it was working to restore the automated system that calculates how much a plane weighs and how that weight is distributed before takeoff. The airline said it was coordinating with air traffic controllers to prevent congestion at gates and on the tarmac in Atlanta.
Hartsfield-Jackson said the disruption was limited to Delta and did not affect airport operations broadly. The airport urged travelers to check their flight status with their airline and arrive at least two hours before domestic flights and three hours before international flights.
The delays at Hartsfield-Jackson came after the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13 because of a technical issue with its air traffic control network. Flights resumed later that evening, but travel disruptions continued through the weekend.
A separate system outage delayed United Airlines departures on Nov. 16, disrupting crew communications and the airline’s ability to send pilots final aircraft weight data, according to the union representing United pilots. United said it resolved the issue that day.
Jay Blackman is an NBC News producer covering such areas as transportation, space, medical and consumer issues.

articles.title_orig: Eisenkot Denounces West Bank Arson
articles.title_zh: Eisenkot Denounces West Bank Arson
articles.content_orig:
Israeli settlers launched a series of attacks across the occupied West Bank, torching at least a dozen cars and vandalizing several homes overnight Sunday, in what Gadi Eisenkot , the main rival of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, decried as “Jewish terrorism.”
Video from the village of Kufr Malik, about 10 miles northeast of Ramallah, the seat of the Palestinian Authority in the West Bank, showed several cars in flames with thick smoke pouring into the sky as a siren blares in the background. In the same village, a home was tagged with Hebrew graffiti, including the word “revenge.”
Similar scenes unfolded in the nearby villages of Deir as-Sudan and Deir Abu Masha’al, two Palestinian communities northwest of Ramallah that were also attacked by settlers.
Mustafa Barghouti, the president of the Palestinian National Initiative, said the brazen attacks were part of an escalating pattern of settler violence.
A rival of Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu calls the recent wave of settler attacks across the occupied West Bank as “Jewish terrorism.”
“Palestinian families are facing violence, destruction and the loss of their homes,” he said on X.
Eisenkot said the violence was the result of the policies of pro-settler, far-right politicians Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who he said “brought the area to the brink of anarchy.” Smotrich was the key architect of a massive expansion of Israeli settlements and outposts in the West Bank over the last four years, while Ben-Gvir has been accused of turning a blind eye to settler violence.
Eisenkot said the attacks were “acts of Jewish terrorism, and we must call them by their name.” Eisenkot, who has four more weeks to attempt to form a government and oust Netanyahu, said the Israeli government should use administrative detention and targeted operations against the assailants.
Netanyahu has not issued any public statement about the attacks. CNN has reached out to his office for comment. Netanyahu has repeatedly tried to downplay settler violence, previously saying it was the result of what he has called “juvenile delinquents.”
The West Bank has seen a surge in settler violence in recent months, particularly around the annual olive harvest, where Palestinians have repeatedly been harassed and attacked. There have been 410 settler attacks related to the olive harvest since the beginning of September, according to the UN.
This weekend’s attacks occurred across several locations in the middle of the night. There were no reports of injuries.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it also received reports of an attack on the Palestinian village of At-Turwani in the southern West Bank near the city of Hebron. The IDF said in a statement it “condemns acts of violence of this nature, which harm public order.” Israeli police said on Sunday they would enter the Palestinian villages under IDF escort to collect evidence. Police have not announced any arrests after the attacks.
Israel faces political chaos as Netanyahu’s grip on power weakens. What will it take to end the disarray?
“Settler terrorism in the West Bank does not take place in a vacuum,” said Yousef Jabareen, the chair of the Arab Joint List party, which saw a surge in support in recent elections. “It is the direct result of the deepening occupation and a government policy under which violence against Palestinians has become an everyday occurrence.”
The attacks on Palestinian villages and sites have not been limited to the West Bank.
On Thursday morning, a mosque in northern Israel was torched and vandalized with graffiti similar to the messages sprayed across Palestinian homes in the West Bank. Pictures shared by Arab lawmaker Ahmad Tibi showed the inside of the mosque burned and charred.
He blamed anti-Arab rhetoric and “people who were poisoned by Netanyahu’s incitement” for the arson.
“The police and the Shin Bet must get to the perpetrators. And immediately,” he said on X.
Zeena Saifi contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: The AI boom is fueling demand for skilled trades
articles.title_zh: The AI boom is fueling demand for skilled trades
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
On weekdays from 5 a.m. to 1 p.m., Marty Tougher clocks in at the construction site of a new building at UPMC Presbyterian, a 900-bed hospital in downtown Pittsburgh.
Depending on the day, he might work on framing — building the skeletons of walls and ceilings — or drywalling to cover that frame with gypsum panels to create finished surfaces.
"It's fun," Tougher, 21, told Yahoo Finance. "I like working with my hands."
Two years ago, Tougher decided to pursue a career as a carpenter, and he's now in his third year in a carpentry apprentice program at the Keystone Mountain Lakes Regional Council of Carpenters in Pittsburgh. The program is tuition-free, combining paid on-the-job training with classroom instruction.
In western Pennsylvania, nonresidential construction is booming with no sign of abating, said Jeff Nobers, executive director of the Builders Guild of Western Pennsylvania.
In high demand are operating engineers, boilermakers, steam fitters, carpenters, plumbers, and electricians. Even some of the trades that weren't necessarily hot a few years back, such as bricklayers, cement masons, roofers, and insulators, are needed again.
"These big billion-dollar data center and natural gas plant projects, for example, require all of them," he said.
Trade jobs are getting renewed traction, driven by infrastructure demand across the country for massive projects like AI data centers, natural gas plants, and power grid expansion.
More than 18 million Americans work in skilled trades, and an expected 1.7 million skilled trade jobs will open each year in the next decade, according to a recent report .
Employment of plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters, for example, is projected to grow 7% from 2025 to 2035, much faster than the average for all occupations, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That adds up to roughly 42,000 openings each year. Plus, retiring workers in these fields are rapidly opening up positions for younger workers.
Apprenticeship programs like the one Tougher is part of generally run from three to five years. Students spend 10% of their time in the classroom, or 200 hours a year, learning specific trade skills along with local building codes, blueprint reading, mathematics, and more. The bulk of their time, 1,800 hours, is on the job, Nobers said.
"What I like about working on construction projects is you can see the progress, how it all comes together, and the work is always changing," said Tougher. "You're not just doing the same thing over and over."
Plus, there are annual raises, healthcare, and pension benefits, he added.
The rising need for trade professionals is in sharp contrast to the overall job market , which is steady but challenging for workers trying to break in. Nearly 2 million people have been unemployed for at least 27 weeks. And the unemployment rate for college graduates ages 22 to 27 soared to 5.2% in September, according to an analysis from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
Still, college remains the most popular path, with more than half of teens considering higher education, while only about 1 in 9 plan to go into the trades after high school.
College graduates generally command higher salaries. The average starting salary for Class of 2025 graduates earning bachelor's degrees was $67,983, according to one recent survey .
The annual median wage for carpenters, for instance, is $60,580. For boilermakers, it jumps to $76,410 .
Don't forget, too, that the average student borrows more than $35,000 to pursue a bachelor's degree, according to a recent analysis by the Education Data Initiative, and it often takes two decades to pay off the debt.
The yearly cost of attendance at more than a dozen colleges is now six figures, after accounting for tuition, fees, room and board, books, transportation, and other incidentals.
That's where trade jobs have an advantage.
"We have to reverse a stigma that has been in place probably a couple decades, driven by a kind of a college-for-all mentality," said Maria Flynn, CEO of Jobs for the Future.
"These are good jobs that pay well, and the shortage that we are looking at as a nation is really significant," she said. "We have a real pipeline problem. For every 100 openings, we're only training 55 workers —  a significant gap."
It's not just high school kids coming in.
"It's younger adults, some who have gone to college or some college and did something else as a potential career out of high school and it didn't pan out, or they realized they were only going to progress so far in that particular field," said Nobers.
There's also the fear of AI coming for jobs, and trades seem somewhat buffered from that concern. While AI will play a role in the construction industry, it's not going to replace the people who physically do the work.
"I don't think we're anywhere near close to the point where AI is going to run an army of robots who build a road," he said. "You still need people to get the work done."
"Both the people going into apprenticeship, but more importantly, their parents … seem to be understanding that these are not, with all due respect to Mike Rowe, dirty jobs."
You have to be technologically savvy, a troubleshooter and a critical thinker, he added. "This is not just, hey, you go out there and hammer nails."
The Department of Labor website, apprenticeship.gov, offers a variety of resources for skilled trade career seekers.
The BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook is a good reference for the fastest-growing occupations, including entry-level education needed, Pay, and job outlook.
Kerry Hannon is a Senior Columnist at Yahoo Finance. She is a career and retirement strategist and the author of 14 books, including " Retirement Bites: A Gen X Guide to Securing Your Financial Future, " " In Control at 50+: How to Succeed in the New World of Work ," and "Never Too Old to Get Rich.

articles.title_orig: Global left rallies in Paris to make ‘not so radical’ case for taxing billionaires
articles.title_zh: Global left rallies in Paris to make ‘not so radical’ case for taxing billionaires
articles.content_orig:
PARIS — The left wants voters to know there is nothing radical about taxing billionaires.
“Radical would be cutting their heads off. But we are not proposing that,” former Chilean President Gabriel Boric told a summit against “international oligarchy” in Paris on Saturday. A minimum tax on the world’s largest fortunes, he said, is “arithmetic.”
Boric was among the left-wing politicians, union leaders and economists brought together by French economist Gabriel Zucman at the Théâtre de la Concorde, a city-owned venue within sight of the U.S. embassy and a short walk from the Elysée.
The gathering drew lawmakers from the U.S. Congress and opposition leaders from Italy, Germany, Britain and the Netherlands, united in the belief that taxing the super-rich could help the left regain the political initiative.
Their pitch was that Zucman’s proposed annual minimum tax of 2% on billionaires’ wealth is a modest measure that most voters already support — and a potent answer to the far right.
“It’s the status quo which is radical,” said Zucman, who cites polls that put support for his tax in France at 86%.
“Remigration will not make your life better, but redistribution will,” said Elly Schlein, leader of Italy’s Democratic Party.
The summit ran for almost 12 hours in a hall the size of a small community theater that was packed for much of the day. Proceedings spilled into corridors and side rooms, where politicians and union leaders from the U.S., Europe and Latin America met between panels.
The event also marked the launch of the Paris Manifesto , a declaration against “international oligarchy” that pairs a minimum tax on the ultra-rich with protections for journalists and a new ownership model for AI companies. More than 100 researchers have signed it, including Nobel Prize-winning economists Joseph Stiglitz, Esther Duflo, Paul Krugman and Daron Acemoglu.
Most of those making the case were out of power, with Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani appearing by video message. Mamdani’s chief of staff, Elle Bisgaard-Church, attended and met European politicians and labor leaders.
The European Commission was not represented, while France’s presidential hopefuls stayed away ahead of next spring’s election. Their parties were represented by figures including Socialist leader Olivier Faure and Éric Coquerel, a lawmaker from the left-wing France Unbowed party who chairs the National Assembly’s finance committee.
The billionaires were present in name throughout the day.
Jesse Klaver, parliamentary leader of Dutch progressive party Pro, opened his speech by saying he had spotted Bernard Arnault — head of French conglomerate LVMH and a frequent target of Zucman’s — on an evening walk in Paris’ tony 8th arrondissement on his way in.
“I [first] thought that you invited him too,” Klaver said. “That would have been a great idea actually, because he could see what energy is here in the room — and that he should be worried.”
Arnault, France’s richest man, has called Zucman a “far-left activist.” The economist said the fight over his tax in France last year showed him the reach of billionaire media owners, who he said control at least 85% of the country’s private press. An LVMH spokesperson declined to comment on Arnault.
Elon Musk drew the most fire. Zack Polanski, leader of the Green Party of England and Wales, said the Tesla chief had called him “a scumbag and a traitor,” and proposed a “Musk tax” on social media companies to fund local news.
Nobel laureate Stiglitz cited Jeff Bezos’ ownership of the Washington Post as an example of the super-rich buying influence over the media. He dismissed warnings that billionaires would stop working if they were taxed: “They want to be top dog, alpha male,” he said.
The U.S. contingent arrived weeks after Democrats won control of Congress in midterm elections and after California voters rejected a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of billionaires.
Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) told POLITICO he will introduce a billionaire tax bill with Bernie Sanders, the independent senator from Vermont, in the first week of the new Congress. “We need to have a fight in the Democratic primary about whether we’ll have a wealth tax,” he said, referring to the 2028 presidential race.
The internal Democratic Party argument on tax is largely settled, said Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) in an interview. “I think we’ve won that debate,” she told POLITICO.
Dave Regan, the union leader behind the California measure, said it lost only narrowly after its opponents spent close to $500 million. He said Gov. Gavin Newsom “should be ashamed of himself” for campaigning against it, and described “a bipartisan consensus at the very top of both political parties to defend the ultra rich.” Regan plans to put a permanent tax to voters in 2028, and is planning referendums in Nevada and Michigan.
Newsom’s office has argued that a state-only wealth tax would drive money and jobs out of California.
Both lawmakers had a message for Brussels, where European Council President António Costa is weighing a tax on U.S. tech giants .
“I think you should be active with your tools,” Jayapal said of the EU’s rules for Big Tech. Khanna called for a transatlantic approach to tax and antitrust, and said “it should not be the United States bullying or dictating to Europe.”
Europe’s left had a fresh win to show off: Dutch lawmakers last week narrowly passed a tax plan that raises wealth taxes to pay for cuts to payroll taxes after two centrist governing parties sided with Pro.
“For the first time, we are going to tax millionaires in the Netherlands,” Klaver said. “A divided left loses. A united left wins.”
Elsewhere, however, the idea is stuck, with the French Senate rejecting Zucman’s tax last year. EU tax laws, meanwhile, need the backing of all 27 governments.
Manon Aubry, co-chair of The Left group in the European Parliament, told POLITICO that a wealth tax should be part of talks on the EU’s next 7-year budget. “The left remains the only, or at least the main, political force that is pushing,” she said.
Dutch Greens MEP Ufuk Kâhya told POLITICO that Europe wants greater security and a stronger economy without settling the question who will pay for it all. Of the European Commission, he said: “They want to eat the cake. But no, you have to also bake it.”
In France, economist Thomas Piketty said a billionaire tax could pass by referendum, on one condition: “We need to win the presidential election. This is the only detail.” The French left has “lots of left-wing candidates. Maybe too many,” he added. France votes next spring.
Critics dispute that diagnosis. François Geerolf, an economist at Sciences Po’s OFCE economic think tank, has argued that Zucman overstates how lightly billionaires are taxed.
But for some in the room, a wealth tax doesn’t go far enough.
“We need to eliminate billionaires, not just tax them,” said author Naomi Klein, who called for a cap on wealth. University of Massachusetts Amherst economist Isabella Weber told POLITICO that “even if we had the most perfect wealth tax, I don’t think it would be enough” without measures to bring down the cost of living.
Regan had a suggestion for billionaires who threaten to leave if they are taxed.
“We should all put our money together and give them the means to get to Mars,” he said.

The southern city of Odesa and surrounding areas have suffered "serious damage" to their main power grids following repeated Russian attacks on critical infrastructure, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo said on Nov. 22.
The electricity supply situation in Odesa Oblast is "extremely difficult" after key power infrastructure supplying households sustained "significant" damage. Repair crews are working to restore electricity, but continued Russian attacks and air raid alerts are disrupting their work, according to Ukrenergo.
"The situation is significantly complicated by constant threats of new attacks and air raid alerts, which prevent repair crews from always working continuously," the company said .
The situation in the Odesa area worsened following the large-scale Russian attack on Nov. 20, after which regional governor Oleh Kiper reported disruptions to the power grids.
The outages have disrupted daily life across the city. Schools in Odesa will switch to online classes for a week starting Nov. 23, local authorities said .
The power cuts have also forced the city to temporarily suspend electric public transportation, including trolleybuses. Local media have also reported disruptions to water and heating supplies.
The damage in Odesa comes as Russia intensifies its attacks on Ukrainian critical infrastructure across the country in recent months, targeting power grids, substations, and water supply facilities as the temperature continues to drop.
Ukraine faces an increasingly severe shortage of Patriot interceptor missiles that can counter ballistic threats, making it difficult for the country to defend itself from the intensifying attacks.
The power and water supply situation across Ukraine, including in Kyiv, has significantly worsened over November, with Russia launching its latest massive aerial assault with missiles and drones on Nov. 20.
The Energy Ministry said on Nov. 22 that Russia attacked an unspecified number of energy facilities over the past day, leaving households in central-eastern Dnipropetrovsk, western Zhytomyr, northeastern Kharkiv, and Odesa oblasts without power this morning.
Of these regions, Odesa Oblast faces the most difficult situation, the ministry said.
"The enemy is purposefully attacking energy facilities important for the region's power supply," the ministry said . "As a result, a significant number of consumers remain without power," it added, without elaborating on the number.
The utility workers managed to partially restore power to critical infrastructure facilities in the Odesa area this morning, and backup power schemes are currently being developed to restore electricity to the rest, according to Ukrenergo.
Asami Terajima is a reporter at the Kyiv Independent covering Ukrainian military affairs and front-line developments. She is the co-author of the weekly War Notes newsletter. She previously worked as a business reporter for the Kyiv Post, focusing on international trade, infrastructure, investment, and energy. Originally from Japan, Terajima moved to Ukraine during childhood and completed her bachelor's degree in Business Administration in the U.S. She is the winner of the Thomson Reuters Foundation's Kurt Schork Award in International Journalism 2023 (Local Reporter category) and the George Weidenfeld Prize, awarded as part of Germany's Axel Springer Prize 2023. She was also featured on the Media Development Foundation's 2023 "25 under 25: Young and Bold" list of emerging media makers in Ukraine. She is among the finalists for the U.K.'s One World Media Award 2026 in the Print category and the French Bayeux Calvados-Normandy award 2025 for war correspondents in the Young Reporter category.
A petition for Kim's resignation has garnered 25,605 signatures, requiring the Cabinet of Ministers to review and respond within 10 days.
"The enemy is deliberately terrorizing the civilian population, attacking civilian infrastructure, and taking lives," Governor Tymur Tkachenko said.
Nine people remain missing as rescue operations continue in Dymer, where a Russian drone destroyed part of a residential building on Nov. 22.
Libyan officials have reported that the Russian Navy corvette Merkury was severely damaged by Ukrainian sea drones. Kyiv has not commented on the claim.
The drills focused on small drones, including first-person-view (FPV) models, Ukraine's General Staff said.
Repair crews are working to restore electricity, but continued Russian attacks and air raid alerts are disrupting their work, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky again urged Washington to authorize the transfer of Patriot missiles that Ukraine's allies have already paid for.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russian troops launched 186 attack drones against Ukraine overnight, of which 161 were shot down.
The number includes 2,310 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
Ahead of the reported attack, a temporary ground stop was imposed at Krasnodar Airport, officials reported, amid the presence of drones in the nearby airspace.
Kyiv and London finalized an agreement on Nov. 21 that will see the United Kingdom manufacture "middle strike" and long-range drones for Ukraine on British soil, Ukraine's Defense Ministry announced.
Both Moldova and Finland reported separate instances of airspace violations by Russia on Nov. 21, officials said, just one day after two suspected Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone fell on Polish territory.
The aircraft were participating in a two-month NATO air defense deployment to protect Polish airspace. Although primarily based in Sweden, the fighters could operate from a forward air base in Poland, according to the Swedish Armed Forces.

articles.title_orig: Coroner's concerns over delays after baby's death
articles.title_zh: Coroner's concerns over delays after baby's death
articles.content_orig:
A coroner has raised concerns about ambulance and medical delays after a 19-day-old baby boy died from sepsis and meningitis.
Sixteen days after Ezrah Pollard's birth in March 2022 he became unwell and was grizzly, not feeding and having a foul nappy.
A Truro inquest heard he developed a fever and a 111 call was transferred to the South Western Ambulance Service Trust (SWAST) which said he needed an ambulance response which should have arrived within 18 minutes.
An ambulance was chased over an hour later but it was not dispatched due to operational pressures - at the time of the incident they were taking four hours on average to respond to cases in the same category.
His parents took him to the Royal Cornwall Hospital in Truro where staff recognised that he was profoundly ill, the inquest heard.
He was transferred to Bristol Royal Hospital the next day where a CT scan revealed a devastating brain injury and he died on 25 March 2022.
Following the inquest, senior Cornwall coroner Andrew Cox wrote a Prevention of Future Deaths report.
He said he was concerned there was no pathway for an infant up to the age of three months to have a Category 1 ambulance disposition.
He said neither the 111 service or ambulance trust could give Ezrah's parents any guidance about the possible delay in an ambulance arrival.
Cox's report added parents should be advised to take a child to hospital immediately but it is understood the scripts followed by telephone dispatchers or non-medically qualified health advisors do not mandate this.
It said: "Ezrah required immediate antibiotics, yet their administration was avoidably delayed."
Ezrah's parents had to repeat details of his condition to the ambulance service and again in hospital because the staff there were not aware of that previous history, which potentially delayed treatment.
Responding to the coroner's report, SWAST said its emergency medical dispatchers (EMD) "do not have sufficient training or expertise to be able to identify a patient with Group B Streptococcus, nor definitely identify a patient with sepsis".
The Trust said they were "not expected to provide a diagnosis based on the symptoms described" and "given they are not clinicians, it would not be appropriate for an EMD to provide self-conveyance advice outside of the Standard Operating Procedure which is used during periods of escalation where we are experiencing capacity pressures due to high demand".
It said it takes the issue of ambulance delays very seriously and significant work has been done with partners to improve response times, but does not give people estimated tome of ambulance arrivals.
The Royal Cornwall Hospitals Trust said there are no extra systems available that would help more effective information sharing than those already in place.
All patients must undergo a formal triage assessment to confirm the patient's identity, current clinical condition and ensure that care is prioritised appropriately and is a key clinical safety measure, a spokesperson said.
Kernow Health CIC, which operates the 111 service in Cornwall said it was "unaware of a restriction in requesting a Category 1 ambulance" and it was "not currently usual practice to advise on waiting times for ambulance arrival".

articles.title_orig: I stopped talking to my husband and let AI do it instead. He didn’t even notice | Polly Hudson
articles.title_zh: I stopped talking to my husband and let AI do it instead. He didn’t even notice | Polly Hudson
articles.content_orig:
What have I learned from my experiment with outsourcing? That I’m easily replaced – and awful
I ’ve just ventured deeper into my phone’s settings than anybody has ever been before. A software update is always discombobulating, but the latest one brought a lot of unwanted AI nonsense (that mental image you just got of me waving my fist at the sky: spot on). Even when you manually switch off Apple Intelligence, check the box to make Siri the same dummy she’s always been, and deselect the option to offer replies to texts and emails, it makes no difference. Harrumph.
Days later, bored on the bus, I began answering my husband’s texts with the terrible suggested AI responses, to see if he’d notice. (We’ve been married a long time; this is how I get my kicks now.)
Mortifyingly, notice he did not. Even when I told him, “You’re a classic!” and laughed “Haha I know right” with nary a comma.
There was worse to come. Because that-which-shall-eventually-rule could tell I’d used its proposed sentences, it was encouraged, and proposed more, which I was tutting and scoffing at until it recommended a reply that ended with the nickname I call my husband. Not darling, honey, or whatever – something unique.
A chill descended in my soul as the penny dropped that these weren’t generic phrases everyone gets – they were specific. My phone was impersonating me, showing me who I really was, and – long story short – I was awful. Cheesy, exclamation-mark-addicted, and full of bantz with a definite z.
Humbled in a way it is probably impossible to ever fully recover from, I realised that in conducting this experiment, I had utilised the very artificial intelligence I was battling to remove just hours before. I’d hate-used it, yes, but I’d used it all the same. Further proof, not that it was needed, that resistance is futile. Luckily I surrendered immediately and have always been fully on board with AI, so when the day comes, I’ll be absolutely fine. Haha I know right.
Polly Hudson is a freelance writer

articles.title_orig: Taiwan warns Canada over dependence on China
articles.title_zh: Taiwan warns Canada over dependence on China
articles.content_orig:
U.S.-China commission leaders warn of growing Chinese military capabilities, threats to Taiwan and risks to American security ahead of Trump’s summit with Xi and Putin.
President Donald Trump faces a potentially dangerous "two versus one" negotiating scenario when he meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, two senior members of a congressional China watchdog warned Wednesday, raising concerns that Beijing could seek concessions on Taiwan while Moscow pushes for greater U.S. pressure on Ukraine.
"I think it is two versus one. We have China and China's junior partner, Russia," Randall Schriver, chairman of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, told Fox News Digital in a Zoom interview. "Largely they come to the table as a team versus President Trump and the United States," he said, citing China's support for Russia's war in Ukraine.
TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES
President Donald Trump greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as President Xi Jinping watches, before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa/Pool via Reuters)
The warning comes ahead of Thursday's planned trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China , on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The high-stakes talks are expected to address issues such as the wars in Ukraine and Iran, trade and nuclear weapons.
Mike Kuiken, the commission's vice chairman, echoed Schriver's assessment, arguing that Moscow's growing dependence on Beijing puts Trump at a disadvantage.
"Putin is a client state of Xi Jinping, and that essentially means that President Trump is in the room with a two against one scenario, and the stakes are significant," Kuiken told Fox News Digital.
"China is fueling Russia's war machine in Ukraine, and they are basically the lifeblood of the Russian economy at this point," he added.
TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA
Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Sputnik/Sergei Bobylyov/Pool via Reuters)
The commissioners spoke as the bipartisan body released its 2026 annual report to Congress , detailing Beijing's expanding military, technological and economic capabilities and the growing challenges they pose to American national security.
Asked what would constitute success or failure at the summit, Kuiken suggested Beijing would not have agreed to the meeting without assurances that its interests would be protected.
"My assessment is that the Chinese would never have agreed to this meeting if they had not had significant assurances that essentially nothing would happen," Kuiken said.
Schriver warned that both Xi and Putin would seek opportunities to advance their strategic objectives. He suggested Beijing would pursue gains related to Taiwan, while Moscow would hope Trump emerged from the meeting prepared to increase pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy .
CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet at the Great Hall of the People on May 14, 2026, in Beijing, China. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
"If Putin had his way, Trump would emerge from the meeting and put more pressure on Zelenskyy," Schriver said.
He also questioned whether sufficient diplomatic groundwork had been laid for meaningful nuclear arms control discussions, one of the issues Trump has indicated he wants to address.
"President Trump would like to talk about nuclear disarmament, probably an agenda that makes sense. I'm just not sure we've done the front-end work when it comes to interagency work, bilateral or trilateral work, at a lower level to have a productive discussion there," Schriver said.
Nevertheless, Schriver suggested that avoiding concessions could itself represent a successful outcome for Washington.
"I think holding ground and just a restatement of U.S. interests is probably a victory of sorts for us," he said.
Responding to the commissioners' warnings, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington defended the trilateral meeting as an opportunity for cooperation among the three powers. "The three presidents will have an in-depth exchange of views on safeguarding world peace and enabling strategic stability in major-country relations. The summit is of groundbreaking significance," the spokesperson told Fox News Digital.
The spokesperson emphasized the three nations' shared responsibilities as permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, arguing that closer communication would serve global stability. "It is in the interest of the three countries to strengthen communication, manage differences and maintain stable relations. This is also the expectation of the international community and is conducive to global stability and dialogue and cooperation," the spokesperson said.
CHINA’S IRAN TIES COMPLICATE TRUMP-XI SUMMIT AS TENSIONS TEST US LEVERAGE
The Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) fabrication plant in Phoenix, Arizona, on March 3, 2025. (Rebecca Noble/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Beyond the summit, the commissioners warned that the United States faces mounting challenges as China approaches 2027, the benchmark year associated with Xi's directive for the People's Liberation Army to develop the capability to conduct a Taiwan military operation.
Asked whether Washington was doing enough to deter Chinese military action against the self-governing island, Schriver gave a blunt assessment.
"I think the short answer is no, we're not doing enough," he said.
Schriver pointed to a pause in congressional notifications for U.S. arms sales to Taiwan , saying the commission wants those notifications to proceed and supports stronger security assistance for the island.
He also warned that Beijing's increasingly sophisticated coercion tactics extend beyond conventional military operations to include actions involving its coast guard.
"We do talk about counter coercion capabilities and blending not only military capabilities but law enforcement that the Chinese are doing, this sort of blended lawfare with their coast guard east of Taiwan," Schriver said.
Taiwanese conscripts during a visit by Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te to a military base in Taichung on June 28, 2024. (Sam YehAFP via Getty Images)
"It's a tough challenge as we're entering the benchmark year that Xi Jinping said of 2027. There should be more attention to this and there should be greater efforts to this."
Kuiken emphasized Taiwan's importance to the global technology supply chain, particularly its role in manufacturing advanced semiconductors used in artificial intelligence.
"Taiwan is the island at the center of the world. Xi Jinping is obsessed with it," he said.
Pointing to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC, Kuiken warned of the broader implications for American technological leadership if Beijing were to take military action against the island.
He urged Washington and its partners to develop a coordinated strategy to make an invasion or other Chinese coercive measures against Taiwan unattractive to Beijing.
President Donald Trump meets with delegations from Japan, India and Australia at the Solaire Hotel, on Nov. 17, 2026, in Manila, Philippines. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
Responding to concerns about Taiwan , a U.S. official told Fox News Digital, "There is no change to our policy with respect to Taiwan." Asked about the commissioners’ warnings, a White House official emphasized President Trump’s diplomatic approach to China and his plans to discuss nuclear arms reduction during the trilateral summit.
"Under President Trump’s leadership, U.S.-China relations have been refocused on what matters most – rebuilding the safety, security and prosperity of Americ

Ukrainian service members took part in a joint drone exercise with forces from the U.S., U.K., Germany, and Latvia to test piloting skills under realistic battlefield conditions, Ukraine's General Staff said on Nov. 22.
The three-day Drone Crucible exercise, organized by U.S. Special Operations Command Europe (SOCEUR), brought together teams to exchange practical knowledge, test drones in field conditions, and provide feedback to manufacturers. The drills focused on small drones, including first-person-view (FPV) models, according to the General Staff.
"For Ukraine, exercises like these provide an opportunity to share lessons from modern warfare with partners, learn from their practices and develop unmanned capabilities together," the General Staff said .
The British Royal Navy said on Nov. 17 that the exercise took place in Bavaria, Germany. Teams from five countries competed in challenges involving strikes on distant targets, reconnaissance, and attacks inside buildings. The U.S. National Drone Association hosted the event.
The exercise comes as Western allies increasingly turn to Ukraine to receive battle-tested drone experience, nearly five years into Russia's full-scale war. As drones increasingly dominate the battlefield, Western armies are working to improve their drone capabilities and piloting skills.
The Ukrainian army regularly participates in multinational exercises to exchange drone knowledge, including at Aurora 26 , a Swedish-led exercise in May where 13 countries took part to learn from the drone war in Ukraine.
Asami Terajima is a reporter at the Kyiv Independent covering Ukrainian military affairs and front-line developments. She is the co-author of the weekly War Notes newsletter. She previously worked as a business reporter for the Kyiv Post, focusing on international trade, infrastructure, investment, and energy. Originally from Japan, Terajima moved to Ukraine during childhood and completed her bachelor's degree in Business Administration in the U.S. She is the winner of the Thomson Reuters Foundation's Kurt Schork Award in International Journalism 2023 (Local Reporter category) and the George Weidenfeld Prize, awarded as part of Germany's Axel Springer Prize 2023. She was also featured on the Media Development Foundation's 2023 "25 under 25: Young and Bold" list of emerging media makers in Ukraine. She is among the finalists for the U.K.'s One World Media Award 2026 in the Print category and the French Bayeux Calvados-Normandy award 2025 for war correspondents in the Young Reporter category.
A petition for Kim's resignation has garnered 25,605 signatures, requiring the Cabinet of Ministers to review and respond within 10 days.
"The enemy is deliberately terrorizing the civilian population, attacking civilian infrastructure, and taking lives," Governor Tymur Tkachenko said.
Nine people remain missing as rescue operations continue in Dymer, where a Russian drone destroyed part of a residential building on Nov. 22.
Libyan officials have reported that the Russian Navy corvette Merkury was severely damaged by Ukrainian sea drones. Kyiv has not commented on the claim.
The drills focused on small drones, including first-person-view (FPV) models, Ukraine's General Staff said.
Repair crews are working to restore electricity, but continued Russian attacks and air raid alerts are disrupting their work, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky again urged Washington to authorize the transfer of Patriot missiles that Ukraine's allies have already paid for.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russian troops launched 186 attack drones against Ukraine overnight, of which 161 were shot down.
The number includes 2,310 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
Ahead of the reported attack, a temporary ground stop was imposed at Krasnodar Airport, officials reported, amid the presence of drones in the nearby airspace.
Kyiv and London finalized an agreement on Nov. 21 that will see the United Kingdom manufacture "middle strike" and long-range drones for Ukraine on British soil, Ukraine's Defense Ministry announced.
Both Moldova and Finland reported separate instances of airspace violations by Russia on Nov. 21, officials said, just one day after two suspected Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone fell on Polish territory.
The aircraft were participating in a two-month NATO air defense deployment to protect Polish airspace. Although primarily based in Sweden, the fighters could operate from a forward air base in Poland, according to the Swedish Armed Forces.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu rival condemns ‘Jewish terrorism’ after settler attacks on Palestinian villages
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu rival condemns ‘Jewish terrorism’ after settler attacks on Palestinian villages
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of militant Israeli settlers raided communities on Saturday night, setting fire to vehicles and several homes
Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank have caused a political row in Israel, drawing condemnation from Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader, who described them as “Jewish terrorism”.
Dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday, setting fire to about a dozen vehicles and several homes and scrawling racist graffiti. At least four communities were attacked. Israeli police said they had launched an investigation with forensic teams.
Photographs from Kafr Malik , near Ramallah, showed one slogan written in Hebrew that read: “This is the first revenge.” Several vehicles and homes had been set alight in the village.
Images from nearby Deir al-Sudan showed vehicles on fire. Palestinian reports said an agricultural building had been set ablaze in Deir Ballut and cars torched in Deir Abu Mashal.
An ⁠inconclusive election last month stripped Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, of his majority. Eisenkot has been asked to form a government, though his prospects seem little better.
“Last night’s arson attacks in Judea and Samaria were acts of Jewish terrorism, in every sense of the term,” Eisenkot said, using the biblical name for the West Bank. “Extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes are undermining regional stability, putting lives at risk and doing grave damage to Israel’s national security and foreign relations.”
Referring to the far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, he added: “The actions led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in the West Bank have brought the area to the brink of unchecked anarchy.”
Eisenkot, who has been given 28 days to form a government by the president, Isaac Herzog, with a possible 14-day extension, urged the government and security establishment to “use every tool at their disposal – including administrative detention and targeted operations by the Shin Bet – to stop the rioters and impose harsh sanctions on them”.
In an unprecedented rebuke on Sunday, several other members of the Israeli parliament criticised Netanyahu over escalating violence by militant settlers against Palestinians.
Yair Lapid, the leader of Yesh Atid, held Netanyahu’s government responsible for encouraging the attacks. “Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence by the Israeli government,” he said on X, adding that ministers were deliberately encouraging the militant settlers’ violence “through their silence”.
Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats party, warned of the possibility of a third intifada and described the West Bank as “on the brink of an explosion”.
“Anyone who wants to prevent a third intifada must replace the current government, which provides cover and support for Jewish terrorism and abandons security,” Golan said on X. “Jewish terrorism harms innocent Palestinians and Israeli army soldiers, and pushes Israel toward unprecedented international isolation.”
Noam Tibon, a retired army major general and Knesset member, gave a similar warning. “If Israel does not eliminate Jewish terrorism in the West Bank, it will destroy Israel,” he wrote.
Netanyahu has not yet responded to the accusations.
Australia announced sanctions on Wednesday against three people and four Israeli entities, including a construction company, over their role in the expansion of illegal settlements and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
A day earlier the UK imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building illegal settlements in the West Bank, which the UN regards as Palestinian territory under Israeli occupation since 1967.
Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.
On Tuesday, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli militant settlers in a village near Jericho, where the group has recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.
Reuters contributed to this report

articles.content_orig:
The S&P 500 entered correction territory after U.S. stocks fell 3.7% Friday, leaving the index more than 10% below its recent peak after it broke its 200-day moving average. Ed Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research and one of Wall Street’s biggest bulls, said the selloff has gone too far and is a correction rather than a bear market, according to BeInCrypto.
Yardeni cited healthy corporate earnings and cheaper valuations, and still expects the S&P 500 to reach 8,500–9,000 by the end of 2027, though he sees no immediate trigger for a sharp recovery. Last year’s Liberation Day crash reversed after Trump changed course on tariffs, but investors may have to wait longer for a rebound this time. Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said inflation remains a serious concern and raised the possibility of a half-point rate hike in December; markets expect further hikes in December and January. UBS strategist David Lefkowitz also expects slower growth and weaker AI spending. U.S. consumer sentiment rose roughly 7% in November to its highest level since August. Upcoming inflation data and December’s Fed decision will test whether rate hikes push the economy toward recession and undermine Yardeni’s recovery outlook.

articles.title_orig: Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz are at the highest levels since the conflict began
articles.title_zh: Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz are at the highest levels since the conflict began
articles.content_orig:
Reported attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz are at the highest levels since the Iran war began, maritime data shows, as Tehran seeks to re-exert its control over the critical waterway amid falling oil prices.
In October, the number of attacks reported to the Royal Navy-affiliated United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) exceeded 30 for the first time since the US-Iran war began in late February.
As of Sunday, at least 22 attacks were reported in November, the second highest figure since the war began, according to a CNN analysis of UKMTO data. The reporting area covers the Strait of Hormuz, the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman.
Before October, the number of reported attacks in the region averaged around 10 per month. Numbers vary, but data from the International Maritime Organization also points to October as having the highest number of confirmed incidents so far this year.
Since the conflict began, the strait has become a heavily contested frontier , with attacks there disrupting oil and gas shipping and sparking global economic fallout.
Iran began trying to halt traffic in the wake of the US-Israeli attacks that launched the war. In response, the US imposed a blockade on Iranian ports, and as CNN previously reported , Gulf producers have found ways of getting ships through the strait.
Commercial traffic through the channel – through which a fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war – remains at a reduced level when compared to the 2025 baseline.
As global oil prices fall and the Iran’s domestic crude revenues come under increasing strain, Tehran has been stepping up attacks, with experts saying the country is losing its leverage over the waterway and could escalate attacks further in an attempt to force concessions from Washington.
The International Energy Agency attributes the recent decline in oil prices to a recovery in Gulf exports. Prices also fell after the US midterm results as concerns over fresh US military action in the Middle East subsided.
“Markets appear to be increasingly assuming that a return to full-scale war is unlikely and that oil supplies will gradually recover,” Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG) think tank, told CNN . “But that assumption could change quickly if Iran decides to intensify the confrontation.”
Meanwhile, Iran’s domestic oil revenues are falling sharply as the US blockade of Iranian ports continues to stifle the country’s supply of oil to global markets, according to maritime data tracking service Kpler.
“Iranian oil on water outside the (US) blockade zone has hit zero as the last cargoes discharged in China earlier this month. Consequently, Iran’s oil revenues could drop to zero by mid-December,” Kpler reported in late October.
US President Donald Trump said this month the US doesn’t “need a deal” with Tehran and ordered Vice President JD Vance to turn his focus elsewhere .
“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed!” Trump posted on Truth Social. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”
He later indicated he wouldn’t hesitate to resume military strikes in Iran if necessary.
During the latest attacks, projectiles struck three tankers exiting the strait on Friday and Saturday, according to Marisks, a maritime risk management company.
Marisks did not confirm who was behind the attacks, though it said Iranian involvement was “assessed as likely.”
Trump says Iran is ‘bullsh*tting’ on effort to end war
Fire erupted aboard the Captain Leon, a Marshall Islands-flagged chemical and oil tanker, after it was struck at the bow at 3 p.m. UTC (10 a.m. ET) on Friday. All crew were reported safe, Marisks said.
The Torkel, a Hong Kong-flagged crude oil tanker, caught fire after being hit in the stern at 5 a.m. UTC on Saturday (midnight ET on Saturday). Less than an hour later, the Arina, also Hong Kong-flagged, was struck in the engine room by a missile.
The attacks demonstrate the “continued critical threat” to commercial shipping in the region, Marisks said, particularly through the “southern corridor” near Oman’s coastline which Iran vehemently opposes.
CNN’s Eleni Giokos, Laura Sharman, Nadeen Ebrahim and Alayna Treene contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Drone attacks kill four near Sudan’s capital, damage UN building
articles.title_zh: Drone attacks kill four near Sudan’s capital, damage UN building
articles.content_orig:
Drone attacks blamed on Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have killed four people in and around the capital, Khartoum, and damaged a United Nations building, according to local reports and UN officials.
The attacks early on Sunday struck residential areas as Sudanese air defences responded to drones reportedly targeting government buildings and Khartoum’s airport.
The strikes have raised fresh concerns about the growing danger to civilians and aid workers as Sudan ‘s war increasingly relies on drones.
Explosions were heard across the capital between approximately 2am (00:00 GMT) and 4:30am (02:30 GMT), according to witnesses cited by the AFP news agency, as the army attempted to intercept the drones.
Al Jazeera’s AlMigdad Alruhaid reported from the city of Omdurman, across the Nile from Khartoum, that three people were killed and nine wounded when a drone struck a home in northern Omdurman.
A child was also killed in a separate attack south of the capital.
In the village of Jebel Aulia, about 45km (28 miles) south of Khartoum, a witness told AFP that a drone hit the home of a mosque official who calls worshippers to prayer. Residents searched the wreckage for trapped relatives.
The UN’s humanitarian coordinator in Sudan, Denise Brown, said on Sunday that one of its buildings had been damaged while staff were inside.
The UN’s humanitarian office, which coordinates emergency relief, condemned the danger to its personnel in a civilian neighbourhood, calling it “unacceptable”.
A Sudanese army source told AFP on Sunday that the drones had been launched from neighbouring Ethiopia’s Bahir Dar airport. The allegation could not be independently verified.
Ethiopia has previously denied Sudanese accusations that it allows the RSF to carry out attacks from its territory.
Sudan has also lodged complaints with the UN Security Council, the body responsible for international peace and security, and the African Union, a continental organisation, over alleged drone operations originating in Ethiopia.
Separately on Sunday, Sudan’s government accused RSF fighters of executing captured soldiers in southeastern Blue Nile state, near the Ethiopian border.
The government condemned the alleged killings as violations of international humanitarian law. The accusation has not been independently verified.
Both the RSF and the Sudanese army are relying more frequently on drones to hit enemy targets. More than 1,100 were killed by drones in the first half of this year, according to the United Nations.
The UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has said that drone attacks account for about two-thirds of children killed or injured in Sudan from the period of January to September.
The war in Sudan between the army and the RSF began in April 2023. It has led to one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with 13 million people displaced and some regions facing famine.

articles.title_orig: Critics cry foul as Israel cranks up deportations of foreign activists in West Bank
articles.title_zh: Critics cry foul as Israel cranks up deportations of foreign activists in West Bank
articles.content_orig:
UN experts on Tuesday expressed alarm over what they described as increasing violence against Palestinian, Israeli, and international human rights defenders in the West Bank . They accused Israel of seeking to remove “critical witnesses” to alleged crimes.
The statement was issued by Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur for the Palestinian territories, and Andrea Bolaños Vargas, the UN special rapporteur on human rights defenders.
“Widespread repression targeting human rights defenders, journalists and protective presence volunteers serves a clear purpose: removing critical witnesses to serious international crimes committed in the context of Israel’s unlawful occupation, settlement enterprise and the ongoing ethnic cleansing of Palestinians,” the experts said.
“Their targeting raises grave concerns for accountability and the preservation of evidence.”
The experts pointed to three recent incidents that they said reflected an escalation in attacks on international observers, journalists, and protective presence volunteers.
They also cited the growing use of arrests, detention, deportation, and exclusion orders against people who accompany Palestinian communities at risk of displacement.
According to the statement, Palestinian activist Ghassan Najjar was arrested in Burin, south of Nablus. He was placed in administrative detention after receiving repeated threats linked to his advocacy for Palestinian farmers during the olive harvest.
The experts also said Israeli journalists and human rights activists Andrey Khrzhanovskiy and Adèle Shoko, along with US journalist Jasper Nathaniel, were violently assaulted near Umm al-Khair in the South Hebron Hills. Some of them were later arrested and served with exclusion orders, the experts said, despite evidence that they had themselves been victims of what the statement called “State-backed settler violence.”
In a third incident, 12 volunteers, two foreign journalists, an activist, and two Palestinian farmers were recently detained during the olive harvest near Kafr Ni’ma, west of Ramallah, according to the statement.
The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) documented at least 16 incidents involving at least 35 Palestinian, Israeli, and international journalists in the West Bank between January and August of this year, up from 13 incidents involving 25 journalists in all of 2025. Nathaniel previously told CPJ that during a stay in Umm al-Khair in early July, a man carrying a club struck him in the stomach and kicked him in the leg.
The experts said the incidents took place as Palestinian communities were increasingly being displaced, and as Israeli officials openly called for permanent Israeli control of the West Bank, expanded settlements, and the displacement of Palestinians.
“The International Court of Justice (ICJ) findings are unequivocal: the occupation is unlawful, and the settlement enterprise is unlawful. Yet, Israel continues to exercise powers derived from this unlawful occupation not only to facilitate the ongoing ethnic cleansing of parts of the Occupied Palestinian Territory, but also to suppress those protecting Palestinian communities and peacefully documenting violations of international law,” the experts said.
“As long as Israel’s unlawful occupation and settlement enterprise remain in place, Palestinian communities and those who seek to protect them will continue to face violence, displacement and repression,” the statement added.
They urged states to use “all available political, economic and diplomatic means” to secure Israel’s withdrawal from the territory and the evacuation of its settlers, in line with the ICJ’s opinion.
“This is the only effective and urgent path to ending the human rights violations endured by Palestinian communities and preventing further attacks against human rights defenders and protective presence volunteers,” they said.

articles.title_orig: I-285 South lanes over Chattahoochee River bridge open after emergency repairs
articles.title_zh: I-285 South lanes over Chattahoochee River bridge open after emergency repairs
articles.content_orig:
Apparent separation on a bridge near South Cobb Drive in Smyrna forced a full interstate shutdown around 8 p.m. Saturday, triggering hours of delays while crews work on repairs and slowly reopen lanes.
COBB COUNTY, Ga. - An issue with a bridge header joint forced hours of emergency lane closures on Interstate 285 southbound in Smyrna on Saturday, according to state transportation officials.
Around 4:25 p.m. on Saturday, GDOT shut down all southbound lanes of I-285 at State Route 280/South Cobb Drive and diverted traffic off the interstate onto South Cobb Drive after Smyrna police reported that the bridge crossing the Chattahoochee River had separated.
After crews inspected the span and reopened multiple lanes, leaving two right lanes blocked for emergency maintenance, GDOT issued a statement Saturday night clarifying that contractors identified an issue with a bridge header joint on the southbound bridge.
"While there is no structural danger to the bridge, the issue has the potential to impact ride quality for motorists," GDOT said in its release.
Contractors are making a temporary repair Saturday night, and GDOT expects all southbound lanes to reopen no later than 10 p.m. However, as of 11:45 p.m., two right lanes are still blocked and the anticipated reopening time is 5 a.m.
GDOT said contractors are scheduled to begin a long-term fix in early December.
Some motorists waited more than two hours to get through the backups before GDOT crews installed a temporary fix, allowing traffic to resume after 10 p.m. Saturday.
"That sounds very dangerous to me," said Tisha Harper. "It sounds like it could be a big hazard."
One driver who was returning home Saturday night said he narrowly avoided the gridlock.
"We just missed it," said Kenneth Duncan. "We came down 75 and took the exit right before, so we were lucky we were coming from South Cobb, not going in the other direction. So fortunately, we missed it, but we know people coming from [the] other direction that got stuck in it."
For others in the area, the Saturday night delays added to ongoing frustration over frequent construction and weekend closures along the interstate.
"Everyone around here has been talking about it, mostly because there’s already been so much traffic on 285 over [the] past couple months, so could you imagine?" said Duncan. "They just keep shutting it down. Every day it seems like there's another thing on 285."
Drivers expressed concern about whether upcoming work could shut down nearby exits or worsen congestion in the surrounding area.
"It seems like every other weekend there’s a big repair going on, so will this add to the list of repairs of 285?" said Duncan. "It looked mostly cosmetic more than anything. When I saw pics, I realized this won't just fall apart."
The driver added that additional detours could strain local roads.
"It's hard for this area," said Duncan. "There's already so much congestion on South Cobb and [the] Paces Ferry area, so more congestion is a tricky thing."
The emergency work adds to an already congested weekend for drivers along the Cobb and Fulton County line.
In a separate, scheduled project just a few miles away, GDOT crews closed the three right lanes of I-285 eastbound over the Chattahoochee River at Powers Ferry Road/Northside Drive (Exit 22) starting at 9 p.m. Friday.
Those eastbound lane closures are scheduled to stay in place until 5 a.m. Monday while crews repair the bridge's concrete overlay, edge beams, substructure and bridge joints.
That $1.6 million preservation project is scheduled to wrap up in late fall 2027.
GDOT has not said what caused the bridge header joint issue to develop Saturday afternoon.
Officials also have not announced exact dates or lane closure plans for the long-term repair scheduled to start in early December.
In the meantime, officials urged drivers to expect delays, reduce their speed and use caution throughout the work zone, and check real-time traffic conditions at 511ga.org or on the Georgia 511 app.
The Source: The information in this story comes from traffic alerts and press releases issued Saturday by the Georgia Department of Transportation and the Smyrna Police Department.

articles.content_orig:
