Iran unveiled a new missile launcher at an underground facility, touting what it says is its continued capability to strike if the war with the United States accelerates once more.
Iranian state television aired footage from an underground missile facility where the paramilitary Revolutionary Guard unveiled a new launcher it said was capable of firing two liquid-fuelled missiles.
The launchers appear to be an advance over a dual launcher that Iran previously used that fired two solid-fuel missiles at a time. Liquid fuel is more efficient and gives operators some capability to adjust the missiles’ speed and trajectory.
The Fars news agency posted a video on X of IRGC commanders visiting what it described as an “underground missile city.”
The location of the missile site was not revealed, but the broadcast aimed to tout Iran’s missile capabilities and counter past US claims to have destroyed the missile programme, amid fears that the war with the US could heat up once again.
During the unveiling of the launchers, Brig Gen Seyyed Majid Mousavi, commander of the Guard’s Aerospace Force, boasted that Iran’s “capabilities have expanded significantly,” adding, “We have integrated ‘surprises’ and highly effective assets into our combat structure.”
At least three oil tankers were attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday in what appeared to be the latest Iranian strikes on shipping through the strategic chokepoint.
The British military’s maritime security centre said in online postings that two tankers were struck separately by projectiles early Saturday while exiting the Persian Gulf through the strait.
One was hit in the stern, the other in the engine room, and there were no reports of casualties, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center reported.
There was no immediate comment from Iran on the centre’s report.
The Iranian Navy said in a statement carried in state media that a tanker hit a naval mine east of the strait before noon and caught fire. State media also said the military carried out its most “intense and varied” operations yet in the strait overnight to stop vessels, aimed at foiling the US military’s efforts to escort shipping through the narrows.
Iranian forces have been attacking shipping through the strait in a campaign aimed at hiking global energy prices to pressure the United States, which has imposed a crippling blockade on Iranian ports.

articles.title_orig: Social Security benefits are rising in 2027, but other changes could affect what you keep
articles.title_zh: Social Security benefits are rising in 2027, but other changes could affect what you keep
articles.content_orig:
Whether you're working or retired, changes to Social Security in 2027 could affect your finances.
Starting in January, millions of program beneficiaries will get a 3.6% increase to their benefits, thanks to the annual cost-of-living adjustment. But rising Medicare premiums could chip away at the increase — and as beneficiaries' incomes rise, that may affect the taxes they owe and their eligibility for a new senior deduction.
Meanwhile, a higher taxable earnings cap means some workers will pay Social Security taxes on more income, reducing their paycheck.
Here's a breakdown of what to expect in the new year.
Social Security's limit for payroll taxes is adjusted every year to reflect the average wage index.
In 2027, the taxable maximum will go up to $192,300 in earnings, up from $184,500 in 2026. Workers and employers each pay a 6.2% payroll tax on earnings up to that limit — or 12.4% for self-employed workers. Medicare taxes of 1.45% for both workers and employers are not subject to a limit.
In 2027, workers who earn $192,300 or more will pay $11,922.60 in total Social Security payroll taxes, according to the Social Security Administration, while self-employed workers will pay $23,845.20.
"If you're somebody whose income is over what the new threshold is going to be, this increase in the threshold results in a tax increase to you," said Tim Steffen, director of advanced planning at financial services firm Baird.
The 3.6% Social Security cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 is slated to increase retirement benefits by about $75 per month on average, according to the Social Security Administration.
The annual adjustment is the largest boost to benefits since 2023 due to rising inflation. The COLA averaged 2.6% from 2000 to 2026, according to the Senior Citizens League , a nonpartisan senior group.
Around 72 million Social Security beneficiaries will see benefit increases, according to the agency.
The maximum benefit for a worker at full retirement age — when individuals become eligible for 100% of the benefits they've earned — will rise to $4,188 per month in 2027, up from $4,152 per month in 2026, according to the federal agency. To be eligible for the maximum benefit at full retirement age — typically age 66 to 67 — you generally have to earn up to the taxable threshold for each of your working years factored into the calculation.
How much of the COLA increase Social Security beneficiaries see depends in part on their Medicare premiums, which may be deducted directly from benefit checks.
Monthly rates are poised to increase for both Medicare Part B, which covers medically necessary services and preventive care, and Part D, which provides prescription drug coverage.
The standard monthly Medicare Part B premium will be $209.40 in 2027 — a $6.50 increase from $202.90 in 2026, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
"It's not often that we see a Part B [premium] increase that is lower than the COLA," Mary Johnson, an independent Social Security and Medicare policy analyst, said of the 3.2% increase. The last time that happened was in 2023, she said.
Medicare Part D beneficiaries may also pay higher premiums in 2027.
Assuming enrollees keep the same plan, the average enrollment-weighted monthly Part D premium may be $51 in 2027, up 50% from $34 in 2026, according to projections from KFF, a provider of health policy research and polling. That is higher than CMS' projections, which forecast the national average premium for standalone Part D plans will rise about $1, to $36, in 2027 from $35 in 2026.
Standard monthly premiums for Part B and plan-specific premiums for Part D apply to individuals who have $112,000 or less in modified adjusted gross income, or $224,000 for married couples. Beneficiaries with higher income pay larger premiums because of income-related monthly adjustment amounts, which affect 9% of Medicare Part B and Part D beneficiaries, according to CMS.
With bigger Social Security benefits, more households may find that some portion of benefits is taxable — though a new senior deduction may help provide some relief to those who are eligible.
Social Security benefits may be subject to federal income taxes for certain individuals. The thresholds at which those taxes are applied are not adjusted from year to year.
Whether or not benefits are taxed is determined by a formula known as combined income — the sum of adjusted gross income, tax-exempt interest income and half of Social Security benefits:
Individuals who are subject to taxes may opt to withhold taxes from their Social Security benefit checks, rather than face a potential bill during tax filing season.
Separately, a temporary senior deduction of up to $6,000 for individuals ages 65 and over may help to indirectly reduce taxes on Social Security benefits.
That deduction, part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025, helps reduce retirees' taxable income, according to Steffen. It's in place through 2028. Because the break phases out for individuals with modified adjusted gross income starting at $75,000 — and for married couples with $150,000 — it's important to watch your income if you're close to those limits, Steffen said.
"Keep in mind that if you're over 65, you might qualify for this deduction," Steffen said. "But if you let your income get too big, you might lose the deduction."
Moreover, any extra income that causes you to lose the deduction may also come with its own taxes, making it more expensive, according to Steffen.
"What we've been telling our clients is that tax planning is a lot more complicated than it used to be, and you can't do it on the back of an envelope anymore," he said. "You need to use good tools that can do good calculations for you."
Individuals who claim Social Security retirement benefits before their full retirement age and who continue to work may be subject to withholdings.
In 2027, individuals under full retirement age may earn up to $25,560 per year, up from $24,480 in 2026, without adjustments to their Social Security benefits. For every $2 in earnings above that limit, $1 in Social Security benefits will be withheld.
Importantly, those withholdings are not lost completely. Once a beneficiary reaches full retirement age, the withheld money will be credited to their benefits over their remaining lifespan.
In the year individuals reach full retirement age, the retirement earnings test limit is higher — $67,920 per year in 2027, up from $65,160 per year in 2026. For every $3 in earnings above that limit, $1 in Social Security benefits is withheld.
Starting the month a beneficiary reaches full retirement age, no earnings are withheld.

articles.title_orig: Russian cargo ship set ablaze in Baltic Sea drifts into Gulf of Finland
articles.title_zh: Russian cargo ship set ablaze in Baltic Sea drifts into Gulf of Finland
articles.content_orig:
Finland says work is continuing on the Sparta II ship on Sunday
Rescue and firefighting efforts are continuing for a Russian cargo vessel hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, authorities have said.
The ship - the Sparta II - was bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday that work was ongoing to make sure the cargo ship did not sink but it was not aware of any danger to surrounding maritime traffic.
Water was still being used to douse the ship on Sunday, and Finland said Estonian and Russian assets were also involved in recovery work.
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used in the strike, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."
The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.
It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Defence Minister Antti HÃ¤kkÃ¤nen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland .

articles.title_orig: Russian Warship Explosion in Libya Destroys Corvette Merkury
articles.title_zh: Russian Warship Explosion in Libya Destroys Corvette Merkury
articles.content_orig:
An explosion has occurred on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port after a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.
The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libyan state media reported, citing the eastern government.
It added that the site was secured, and there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.
Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC, reviewed by BBC Verify, shows a boat on fire at 0547 GMT at the Benghazi port, with a separate image captured several hours later appearing to show the same vessel partially submerged.
Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship engulfed in flames and smoke, while it is still dark.
The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.
GNS said the country was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.
Seperately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.
GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".
Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.

articles.title_orig: 26-year-old Google worker earns $323,000 a year—but lives on less than minimum wage
articles.title_zh: 26-year-old Google worker earns $323,000 a year—but lives on less than minimum wage
articles.content_orig:
This story is part of CNBC Make It's Millennial Money series, which details how people around the world earn, spend and save their money.
At 26 years old, Google AI security analyst and YouTuber Charles Broomfield is on track to earn about $323,000 this year — but he lives on less than minimum wage.
For the past few years, Broomfield has kept his annual spending on core living expenses under $20,000, less than the roughly $23,700 a full-time worker would earn at the minimum wage, averaged across all 50 states.
He does it by living with roommates in Washington, D.C., walking or biking instead of driving, eating free meals at work and rarely spending beyond his basic needs. Even when he splurges on something fun, he keeps things modest; in August, that meant a baseball game and a single $7 beer.
"I guess something else that probably does make me a little bit unique is I really don't feel joy when I buy things," he says. "I feel like I have what I need."
There is a goal behind all that saving. Broomfield has pursued financial independence since college and now expects to reach his target of $750,000 in investments within the next year, well ahead of his original goal of doing so by age 30. As his income has climbed, his lifestyle has largely stayed the same, he says.
Here's how Broomfield keeps his spending so low and what he plans to do once he no longer needs the paycheck.
Broomfield grew up in Colorado Springs, Colorado, the son of two military veterans. He and his siblings had to set aside half of everything they earned growing up. They could spend the other half or earn interest from their parents by putting that money away, too.
By his teenage years, Broomfield had become a disciplined saver. At the time, he dreamed of using his cash stash to buy some of the familiar trappings of wealth.
"I wanted a Lamborghini and I wanted some nice penthouse," he says. "I just wanted them because I thought other people wanted them."
At 17, Broomfield discovered Mr. Money Mustache, a personal finance blog by a former software engineer who retired at 30. The blog advocates living frugally and investing much of your income to build a portfolio large enough to support you through withdrawals, without needing a paycheck. It introduced Broomfield to the financial independence, retire early — or FIRE — movement and gave all that saving a new purpose.
"All I had to do was live super frugally and I could actually reach financial freedom by the time I was 30 and go do whatever actually made me happy in life," he says.
The idea stuck with him. After graduating from Knox College in 2022, Broomfield moved to Northern Virginia for a job paying more than $100,000 a year and set a goal of reaching $750,000 in investments before 30 while spending less than $25,000 a year.
He also decided to start at $0. Broomfield had roughly $50,000 in savings when he graduated, with his parents having covered the portion of his college tuition not paid for by scholarships. He wanted his FIRE total to reflect only what he earned after college.
In his first year after college, Broomfield was "super geeked out" about reaching financial freedom, he says.
"It's almost the only thing I thought about, because I was building all these new habits and making real money for really the first time in my life," he says.
That enthusiasm sometimes took him to extremes. He even considered living in a van parked in his employer's garage to avoid paying rent.
"I crunched the numbers on it, and effectively every year that I spent living in a van rather than paying rent would allow me to retire approximately one month faster," he says. "It just [didn't] seem really worth it to go to that extreme."
But Broomfield still found satisfaction in squeezing every dollar out of his budget. He once biked two miles to a grocery store to save $1 on toothpaste rather than buy it at the Whole Foods next to his apartment.
"For a lot of people, they feel their wins by buying stuff for themselves," Broomfield says. "I get my wins by seeing how much I can invest."
Looking back, Broomfield acknowledges that some of his early efforts to save money made little difference in how quickly he could reach financial independence.
"I never expect anybody else to do exactly what I'm doing," he says. "I know I'm way more of a geek about this than most people, and I'm particularly well positioned to be able to live this kind of life."
Broomfield's core living expenses totaled $1,477 in August, excluding savings, investments and payments toward his graduate school tuition.
Here's a breakdown of where his money went that month, including those additional payments:
Roughly 90% of Broomfield's income went to savings and investments in August, a fairly typical month for him, he says. He put about $7,931 into his 401(k) and another $10,000 into a taxable brokerage account.
Another $700 went toward a 0% interest employer tuition repayment plan with a former employer, leaving him with a remaining balance of $16,800 in August.
Housing is Broomfield's biggest expense, though he keeps costs down by sharing an apartment with four roommates. In a neighborhood where one-bedroom apartments commonly rent for more than $2,000, the arrangement saves him about $1,000 a month.
One thing Broomfield is willing to splurge on is a martial arts gym membership. He pays $229 a month to train as a kickboxer, even though he could work out for free at Google's office gym. Broomfield considers it a "young person's sport" and doesn't want to postpone competing until after he reaches financial independence. It's also a way to socialize with other amateur fighters who share his interest.
Broomfield doesn't own a car and generally walks, bikes or takes public transportation. Google covers his daily Metro commute, which helps keep his transportation costs low. He tries to meet friends near Metro stations and, when visiting his grandfather in Virginia, takes public transit as far as he can before using Uber for the last leg of the trip.
Before joining Google, Broomfield typically spent around $200 a month on food. Now that he eats most of his meals at work , he spends about $70 a month on average. His $28 food bill in August was especially low because he had ingredients left over from July.
He also cooks less at home these days. Previously, he relied more on batch cooking, including pressure cooker chili that makes nine servings for about $2 each. For snacks, he might have a bowl of Raisin Bran or celery with peanut butter.
“I did the math once, and peanut butter was the lowest cost thing per gram of protein in the entire grocery store,” he says in a video on his YouTube channel, which he started in 2023 to document his FIRE journey.
For entertainment, he relies on the free version of YouTube, where he watches educational content about startups, business and entrepreneurship, or listens to music.
Broomfield expects to make about $323,000 in 2026, more than triple the roughly $100,000 he earned in his first year out of college. His compensation rose to about $120,000 over his first three years, then jumped to $200,000 when he joined Amazon Web Services in 2025. After a brief stint at Capital One, he moved to Google this year. By keeping his expenses low, investing most of what he earns and riding an upward-trending stock market, he has built up about $650,000 in investments since graduating from college.
Broomfield earns money from his YouTube channel as well, which has expanded to offer personal finance and career advice. About $48,000 of his projected income this year will come from the channel and a related career-coaching business.
Even as his income has grown, Broomfield has stuck with roommates, public transportation and the same modest spending habits.
"I've really separated how happy I am from how much money I spend," he says. "I truly don't believe that I would be significantly happier if I spent a lot more money."

articles.title_orig: GTA 6 Glitch Unlocks The FPS On Xbox Series X|S, But With Multiple Drawbacks
articles.title_zh: GTA 6 Glitch Unlocks The FPS On Xbox Series X|S, But With Multiple Drawbacks
articles.content_orig:
If there's anything we could add to GTA 6 as things stand, it'd be an official 60FPS mode. That's obviously not possible right now due to how demanding the game is on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S hardware, even in the case of the PS5 Pro.
Interestingly though, over the weekend, players have discovered the ability to activate what some are calling a "60FPS Glitch" or "60FPS Bug" on Xbox consoles, forcing the game to unlock its FPS and run at a higher frame rate than it's actually supposed to.
Someone called Meowwie64 on Reddit appears to have found this, and here's what they did to activate it:
Now, as mentioned, there are multiple drawbacks here. The first one is that the glitch speeds up most aspects of the game, making it run faster than intended (and look like it's in fast-forward mode!). This is obviously not an ideal way to enjoy GTA 6, and serves as an immediate deal-breaker in my view.
Another one is that reaching 60FPS is pretty much impossible under normal gameplay circumstances. If you're driving down a highway, for example, you're likely only going to get around 35-40FPS at max, with 60FPS and above being saved for situations that require no graphical intensity whatsoever.
And finally, it should be noted that GTA 6 was never intended to be run this way on Xbox Series X|S, and therefore you could run into all sorts of issues - crashes, bugs, maybe even your console overheating. That last one is unlikely, but the game has been specifically built to run at 30FPS on these machines, so it's not worth pushing it in our view.
We'll leave you with some footage of this glitch running on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S down below (courtesy of the always-excellent Fuzion Xbox Testing ), and prepare for it to be officially fixed in an upcoming GTA 6 update.

articles.title_orig: Trump says he'd work with Dems to cap credit card interest, fees
articles.title_zh: Trump says he'd work with Dems to cap credit card interest, fees
articles.content_orig:
President Trump said he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates, hoping to fulfill a promise he made on the 2024 campaign trail but couldn't deliver on because of industry pressure and a lack of interest from his fellow Republicans.
"I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump told Fox News Channel's "Saturday in America."
Democrats and the Republican president have both backed capping credit card interest rates, with the standard proposal being capping rates at 10%. It would substantially reduce what credit card companies can charge customers. The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve.
With rates at 10%, a cardholder with a $5,000 balance would pay about $42 per month in interest. At the current average rate of 22%, they would owe about $100 per month.
Mr. Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates in January , as part of the White House's affordability push. Banks and credit card companies immediately and aggressively opposed the proposal, saying any interest rate cap would force them to cancel cards for the poor and less creditworthy customers or substantially cut back on the rewards they offer when customers spend on their cards.
The proposal also did not sit well with Republicans, and there was little effort by the GOP-controlled Congress to fulfill Mr. Trump's promise.
That could change now that Democrats will control both the House and Senate. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who is expected to be the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has said repeatedly she wants to cap rates .
In response to the Fox News interview, Warren said: "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money." Warren told CBS News in January 2026 that she believes Congress could work with Mr. Trump to cap rates.
Researchers who studied Mr. Trump's campaign pledge after it was first announced found that Americans would save roughly $100 billion in interest a year if credit card rates were capped at 10%. The same researchers found that while the credit card industry would take a major hit, it would still be profitable, although credit card rewards and other perks might be scaled back.
About 195 million people in the United States had credit cards in 2024 and were assessed $160 billion in interest charges , the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says.
Americans are now carrying more credit card debt than ever, to the tune of about $1.23 trillion, according to figures from the New York Federal Reserve for the third quarter last year.

articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Like SpaceX, Anthropic ran an unusual IPO process, chafing some bankers
articles.content_orig:
By Jack Delaney – Nov 22, 2026 at 3:09PM EST
10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›
After nearly every initial public offering (IPO), insiders and pre-IPO stakeholders have to wait for a period before they can sell shares on the open market. These lockup periods can last for up to a year, but their expirations always cause some concern among new shareholders. After all, if insiders flood the market with their shares and demand from buyers doesn't keep up with supply, it can put downward pressure on the stock price.
For Anthropic ( ANT -8.50% ) , which went public on Nov. 19, employees and executives will eventually have the opportunity to sell more of their shares. But instead of lockup periods ending, there are higher priorities for shareholders to focus on.
Image source: Getty Images.
If employees start selling when a lockup period ends, that shouldn't be viewed as an automatic red flag or a signal that they have lost faith in their company. Rather, it's one of the first times they can turn the paper wealth they've accumulated over the years into actual liquid wealth.
For Anthropic, the lockup expirations are more staggered than a traditional IPO, with shares unlocking at several intervals over the next year — including one that took place Friday unlocking up to 315 million shares, and several more large events over the next couple of months. That just means that, instead of one selling date to focus on, there will be multiple selling points. That's important to note for anyone planning to invest in Anthropic, as they may see some choppy price action around those dates.
That said, lockup-related volatility is typically a short-term factor. The bigger drivers of the stock price over the long term will be revenue growth, spending, and profitability.
Anthropic is showing explosive top-line growth.
Revenue jumped roughly 1,200% in the first nine months of 2026 to $33.2 billion, and it now has approximately 250 customers spending $10 million or more on a 12-month trailing basis. In addition, its net revenue retention rate of approximately 900% as of Sept. 30 shows that existing customers are dramatically increasing their spending with Anthropic over time. These types of numbers support the case of a rapidly expanding business that can become more valuable.
However, while rising revenues are good, there is also something to watch out for: spending. In its S-1 filing, Anthropic disclosed that it has committed to  $895.4 billion in spending in the coming years, largely connected to infrastructure and compute. And of that spending, around $447.5 billion is expected to occur before 2030. If demand for artificial intelligence (AI) slows or if competitors win market share away from Anthropic’s models, these costs could become a financial drain.
Aside from revenue growth and spending, Anthropic is still losing money, reporting a net loss of $25.1 billion for the first nine months of 2026. But its losses are shrinking, as its net loss was $104 billion for the first nine months of 2025.
The bull case for Anthropic as an investment is that it will keep turning widening AI adoption into growing revenues, which it could eventually convert into profits. The bear case is that demand for Anthropic’s models and tools won’t be as great as the company is anticipating, or that it starts losing market share. Either case would ultimately leave its massive spending unjustifiable.

articles.title_orig: Delta says ‘automation’ issues causing delays in Atlanta, nationwide
articles.title_zh: Delta says ‘automation’ issues causing delays in Atlanta, nationwide
articles.content_orig:
ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — Delays are mounting across the country for Delta Air Lines flights after a ground stop and ground delay caused by a technical issue, the Atlanta-based airline said.
A ground stop issued Sunday morning for Delta flights on their way to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport turned into a ground delay, the FAA said Sunday.
The ground delay, which is in effect until at least 1 p.m., means that flights on the ground heading to Atlanta will now be allowed to depart, but they are being delayed nearly an hour.
The ground delays are due to a problem with Delta’s weight and balance automation system, the Atlanta-based airline said.
“Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation,” the airline said.
Because flights are taking longer to depart due to Delta personnel having to manually calculate their weight, it is limiting gate space for arriving flights, exacerbating the delays.
“We are working with our air traffic control counterparts to strategically enact programs to protect airport gates and tarmac areas from congestion at our Atlanta hub,” Delta said.
Delta passengers are reporting delays at multiple US airports online, including Atlanta, Newark, LaGuardia, Reagan National, Dulles, Boston, Baltimore, Miami, Minneapolis, Nashville, San Antonio, Birmingham.
Just before 10 a.m., nearly 500 flights were delayed at the airport, according to FlightAware , a flight tracking website.
The delays come just as the busy Thanksgiving travel period is about to begin. Officials at Hartsfield-Jackson airport expect more than 4 million passengers through Dec. 1, up 5% from last year.
READ: Hartsfield-Jackson airport expects 4 million passengers during Thanksgiving holiday travel
Just days ago, a nationwide ground stop caused mass cancellations at the world’s busiest airport.
Atlanta’s airport General Manager Ricky Smith said the nationwide ground stop told Atlanta News First that the incident was a “big test” as Thanksgiving travel nears.

articles.title_orig: Correction or deeper reckoning? Investors seek signs US stock selling will abate
articles.title_zh: Correction or deeper reckoning? Investors seek signs US stock selling will abate
articles.content_orig:
The S&P 500 lost 8.6% this week and closed 6% below its 200-day average. Earnings haven’t cracked, which makes this a liquidity event. The question is whether the Fed blinks before the break hardens.
Last week, in VIX Spike: Complacency’s Bill Coming Due , we warned that low volatility eventually begets high volatility. That bill came due early. The S&P 500 fell 8.6% to 6,910, its seventh straight losing session and the longest losing streak since February 2020. The Nasdaq-100 dropped 10.4%, the Dow lost 8.0%, and the Russell 2000 slid 7.5%. At 11.6% below its October 6 record, the index is in “correction” territory, and the VIX nearly doubled to 37.
So was this a liquidation of leveraged positions due to margin calls? Partly, but not the way the headlines suggest. FINRA’s latest data put margin debt at $1.45 trillion in October, down 2.1% from September and 3.6% below June’s record. Margin borrowing was already easing before the week began.
What we saw instead was mechanical deleveraging. On Thursday, just 38 S&P 500 stocks rose while 464 fell, and all 11 sectors finished lower, even staples. Goldman’s Rich Privorotsky called it “a pretty violent liquidation” in a note covered by ZeroHedge. Dealers were heavily short gamma into Friday’s monthly options expiration, which fed the afternoon selling. Desk chatter also had investors selling gold, copper, crypto and Nvidia to fund allocations in Anthropic’s IPO , which priced at $83 on Wednesday. Gold fell 9.5%, copper 10.2% and Bitcoin broke below $60,000.
Macro supplied the trigger. Fed Governor Christopher Waller called for a 50-basis-point hike at the December 8-9 meeting after a third straight 0.3% monthly gain in core CPI. The Commerce Department’s rule restricting remote access to advanced AI chips by Chinese firms took effect on Thursday, landing on the AI supply chain the same day. Meanwhile, the 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.91% from 5.15%. The bond market is starting to price a growth problem, while the Fed is still fighting an inflation problem.
Here is the real question that needs an answer. “Have the fundamentals changed?” Not yet. Through FactSet’s November 13 update, analysts had raised fourth-quarter EPS estimates 1.1% since September 30, something that rarely happens mid-quarter, and third-quarter earnings grew 31.9%.
The Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow still tracks fourth-quarter growth at 3.4%, and initial jobless claims of 203,000 remain near historic lows. Cracks are showing only at the edges. The Philadelphia Fed index collapsed to 6.3 against expectations of 20, the Conference Board’s leading index fell 0.3%, and existing home sales hit their slowest pace since 2010. So far, this is a valuation and liquidity event, not an earnings recession. At 6,910, the S&P 500 trades near 16.6 times FactSet’s November 5 forward earnings estimate of $415.82, down from 17.7 times on that date.
This suggests that the liquidation of positions is likely “overdone.” Since 1950, the S&P 500 has suffered 17 separate episodes in which it fell 8% or more over five sessions. It was higher three months later in 15 of them, with a median gain of 8.1% . The catch is that the median further drawdown along the way was 4.5%, so the bottom rarely arrives on schedule.
Next week, the main focus will be on the Federal Reserve. If Wednesday’s PCE data cools and Fed speakers soften, the setup for a reflexive rally is in place. If not, Privorotsky’s 2018 comparison, when the Fed kept hiking and stocks didn’t bottom until Christmas Eve , becomes the playbook .
The S&P 500 closed Friday, November 20, at 6,910.39, down 8.6% for the week. That leaves the index 6.0% below its 200-day average at 7,348.58 and 9.4% below its 50-day average at 7,625.25. It closed below the lower 2-standard-deviation Bollinger Band at 7,094. It also finished just 18 points above the lower 3-SD band at 6,892. To wit: the index ended the week 2.9 standard deviations below its 20-day mean.
The technical backdrop is telling a more interesting story. First, momentum is confirming the extreme selling pressure this past week. On Friday, the 14-day RSI fell to 24.7. That is its lowest reading since April 8, 2025. That date is important as it marked the bottom of the tariff-driven selloff. Notably, during that selloff, the market was being priced for an impact on earnings growth from tariffs. However, currently, analysts continue to maintain or raise earnings estimates for the fourth quarter and next year.
Secondly, the MACD sits at −130 index points, well below its signal line at −75, and Williams %R is at −97. Such is what a forced-selling week looks like on a chart. Oversold is a condition, not a buy signal, and it can persist longer than anyone expects during a liquidation.
Third, breadth tells a more nuanced story. The equal-weight S&P 500 fell 6.1% against 8.4% for the cap-weighted S&P 500 index. The damage has been largely concentrated in the AI complex, with Technology falling 12.3%. However,  semiconductors (SMH) dropped 17.8%, while Nvidia lost 22.9%.
Even the more defensive sectors couldn’t avoid the selling pressure. Staples and Utilities lost 2.0% and 3.0%, respectively. In other words, defensive stocks did their job of reducing the volatility, but they didn’t avoid it. The average stock is in better shape than the index, which helps any rebound broaden. But leadership is what broke, and leadership rarely heals in a week.
Volatility and bonds tell you what kind of selloff this is. The VIX closed at 37.24, nearly double last Friday’s 19.30. Meanwhile, the 10-year Treasury yield fell 24 basis points, and the long-bond ETF (TLT) gained 2.6% while nearly everything else fell. When bonds rally as stocks drop, investors are running from risk rather than scrambling for cash. Watch that relationship next week. If Treasuries start selling off alongside stocks, the liquidation has moved into a more dangerous phase.
In our portfolios, we used the decline to nibble on NVDA and PANW this week. However, these were very small additions, and something that we will likely continue to do into further weakness. Notably, these are NOT calls that the market has bottomed. Next week, we’ll trim value positions to raise cash. That keeps the dip buys from adding to overall equity exposure while the index sits below a level that matters this much. Our 7,000 risk line gave way on Friday, and we’re treating it that way.
For more aggressive traders, the playbook is to let the rubber band snap before acting. With the market at a 2.9-standard deviation (SD) extreme, a reflexive rally toward the lower 2-SD band near 7,094 should be expected. That is a tradeable reflex rally, but should be treated as a strict trade with defined exits.
The 200-day average at 7,349 is the first real test above the market currently. For now, use any rallies into that zone to rebalance and reduce risk rather than chase. However, on the downside, the 3-SD band at 6,892 is only a thin level of support. Any decisive break opens the April 7 close of 6,617, where the spring rally launched.
Next week, there is only one market level that really matters: 7,349. Any snapback toward the 200-day average would be normal from an oversold extreme this deep. What matters is whether the index can close and hold above it. That action will decide whether this break joins the healed ones or the deep breaks that keep going.
This coming week, Thanksgiving will compress everything into just three trading sessions. Markets are closed on Thursday, and then the market will close early at 1:00 p.m. ET on Friday. For investors, this is a week to turn off monitors and enjoy your family, as the thin holiday trading tends to magnify moves in both directions. With the VIX sitting at 37, this is where investors tend to make mistakes.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Stocks Extend Plunge as AI Boom Turns to Bust
articles.title_zh: U.S. Stocks Extend Plunge as AI Boom Turns to Bust
articles.content_orig:
A punishing sell-off in technology stocks intensified Friday, wiping out the Nasdaq Composite’s gains for the year, as investors continued to pull money out of the once high-flying AI trade.
The S&P 500 fell 3.7% and posted its seventh consecutive day of losses — its longest losing streak since February 2020, when Wall Street started bracing for what became the Covid pandemic.
The tech-focused Nasdaq faced even steeper losses on Friday, dropping 5.28%. It is now down more than 2% for the year.
The Nasdaq hit a record high on October 6, and was up as much as 18.7% on the year. Since that all-time high, the index has slumped, erasing all those gains and shedding roughly $8.7 trillion in market value.
“It’s a meltdown right now,” Arun Sundaram, senior vice president of investment strategy at CFRA Research, told CNN in an email. “So much bearish sentiment around tech and AI.”
Even Anthropic’s blockbuster stock market debut quickly lost its shine Friday, with shares in the AI lab dropping 8.5%. They closed at $88.91, just above the company’s IPO of $83.
Why Anthropic’s blockbuster debut didn’t ease Wall Street’s AI fears
The Dow fell 950 points, or 1.93%, posting its fifth consecutive day of losses of more than 1%. The Dow dropped 8% this week, its worst week since March 2020.
The Dow and the S&P 500 closed in correction on Friday, trading down more than 10% from their respective peaks on August 5 and October 6. They join the Nasdaq, which closed in correction earlier this month and is now down 18% since its record high on October 6.
Meanwhile, the Nasdaq and S&P 500 suffered their worst week since early April 2025, when President Donald Trump’s tariff plans rocked global markets.
Stocks associated with the AI trade have been in a serious rough patch for weeks now. But with Anthropic’s buzzy IPO now in the rear-view mirror, traders’ concerns about the broader industry are once again coming to the fore.
It’s the year of the mega AI IPO. Should you invest?
“There is a real exodus out of tech stocks,” Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at the online brokerage platform Interactive Brokers, told CNN. “Buy the dip has been taking a back seat to sell the rally – or just sell.”
“The tech sector is just getting walloped,” Sosnick said.
Investors are grappling with a bevy of concerns, from uncertainty over how newly elected Democratic governors will impact the pace of the data center buildout to uncertainty about the future of Nvidia’s role in powering the AI industry’s growth after CEO Jensen Huang resigned.
“There is a fear that maybe there is too much froth and enthusiasm in the tech bet given all the risks out there,” said David Kelly, chief global strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management.
Kelly noted that corrections are “inevitable” and there is “nothing particularly ominous” about a correction given how much US stocks have rallied in recent years.
“This is not a fatal illness. It’s not even the flu. At the moment, it looks like a mild cold, and it should be over in a week or two,” he said.
Another growing concern for investors: Companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on the AI buildout, using their own cash and also tapping the debt and equity markets to raise more capital.
For awhile, investors cheered the AI spending. But now, they’re getting more serious about demanding evidence of return on investment.
“The market was already questioning some of the cost-benefit analysis … and you’re coming off of relatively euphoric levels. Put all that together, that’s a lot for the market to bear,” Sosnick at Interactive Brokers told CNN.
In a sign of growing nervousness among investors, the VIX, which tracks expectations for volatility and is known as Wall Street’s ‘fear gauge,’ surged 86% this week and closed at 35.89 on Friday — its highest level in 19 months. Generally, a level above 20 indicates heightened investor uncertainty.
The sell-off sent investors looking for safer corners of the market, like US Treasury bonds, which rallied sharply on Friday.
Corners of the AI trade that have been in the spotlight in recent weeks were among the names under pressure. CoreWeave, the neocloud backed by Nvidia, slumped 12% Friday. CoreWeave’s IPO price in March 2025 was $40 a share — it’s trading at $39.51 now, wiping out all gains since it debuted on the market.
Trump defends Putin relationship and says he’ll stop US companies from building data centers abroad
Nvidia dropped 14% on Friday, its worst day in almost two years. The chip giant tumbled 22.9% on the week, posting its worst week since October 2008.
Reuters reported Friday that the US Securities and Exchange Commission is probing Nvidia over its accounting practices, adding to pressure on the stock.
Nvidia has plunged 47.5% since its October 6 peak, shedding $2.7 trillion in market value. That’s larger than the individual market value of every company in the S&P 500 except Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet and Nvidia itself.
The sell-off has been so severe that tech stocks may suddenly look cheap to some investors. US tech stock valuations, as measured by the forward price-to-earnings ratio of the S&P 500’s info tech sector, entered Friday at their lowest level since March 2020, according to FactSet.
As for Nvidia? The forward P/E ratio for the next 12 months is the lowest since 2002.
That has some strategists suggesting that widespread fears might be overblown.
“I don’t fully understand it, as the fundamentals don’t really justify all this selling,” said Sundaram from CFRA Research. “But right now, it’s sell now and worry about the fundamentals later.”

articles.title_orig: One Type of Exercise Could Be an Overlooked Treatment For Knee Osteoarthritis, Clinical Trial Finds
articles.title_zh: One Type of Exercise Could Be an Overlooked Treatment For Knee Osteoarthritis, Clinical Trial Finds
articles.content_orig:
Pain, swelling, and stiffness in the knees can be downright debilitating.
As cartilage breaks down in these joints, it can significantly reduce freedom of movement and cause pain, even when standing still or sitting.
Surprisingly enough, core exercises may be a neglected form of treatment for knee osteoarthritis.
A randomized controlled trial in India has now found that working out the abdominal muscles may have a trickle-down effect for the knees.
Strengthening the abdomen won't stop cartilage from degenerating, but in this particular trial, when core exercises were added to typical rehabilitation programs, it improved physical function more than conventional exercises alone.
What's more, patients who did the core exercises also reported significantly less pain when moving about.
The findings are published in Scientific Reports , and while the study is small, the methodology was rigorously designed.
The trial involved 100 participants, aged 40 to 80, with mild to moderate knee osteoarthritis.
Roughly half the group were randomized to partake in conventional knee-focused rehabilitation for 12 weeks.
During the trial, this half of the group partook in 45 minutes of supervised exercise three times a week for four weeks.
Each session involved progressive strengthening, range-of-motion, and functional exercises, such as straight-leg raises and moves to strengthen the quadriceps.
Participants then continued these exercises at home on their own for an additional 8 weeks.
Meanwhile, the other half of the group was randomized to undertake a different rehabilitation program.
This one involved a mix of conventional knee-based rehabilitation exercises and progressive core-targeting exercises.
The core exercises included abdominal bracing, glute bridges, forearm planks, arm raises while lying down, heel taps, and alternating arm-and-leg movements similar to dead bugs.
After the 12-week intervention period, both groups demonstrated significant reductions in resting pain.
But it was the group that also partook in core training that demonstrated greater improvements in physical function tests and reported less pain when moving about.
Importantly, this group also reported greater improvements in their quality of life.
The authors of the study don't know why core training led to these benefits, but they suggest that an improvement in posture control may help stabilize the body's core during exercise, putting less strain on the lower limbs.
"Collectively," the team concludes , "these biomechanical adaptations provide a plausible explanation for the greater improvement observed in pain, physical function, and quality of life compared with conventional knee-focused strengthening alone."
The findings are supported by previous research, which also suggests that the core is a neglected part of knee pain.
In 2021, for instance, a peer-reviewed narrative review argued that despite preliminary findings that core training is beneficial for knee issues, more research is needed.
"Investigations that show it is safe and effective in older adults have not been adapted to/incorporated into treatment recommendations for those with knee osteoarthritis," the authors argued.
This year, the results of several randomized clinical trials have begun to roll in.
One trial among 48 patients with knee osteoarthritis in Pakistan, for example, also found that adding core stability training to knee exercises produced greater improvements in pain, knee mobility, and quality of life after 12 weeks.
Plus, a larger study of 100 patients found that adding core exercises to conventional knee rehabilitation was more effective than adding foot-and-ankle strengthening.
That seemed to be particularly true for outcomes like pain and physical function.
Related: Study of 33,500 CT Scans Challenges a Common Assumption About Ab Strength And Back Pain
These randomized trials are small, but their findings suggest that exclusively targeting the joints during osteoarthritis treatment may not be the best move.
The whole body is connected, and the function of our extremities is founded upon the stability of our trunk.
Ab exercises may help cut to the core of the issue.
The research has been published in Scientific Reports .

articles.title_orig: What to know about US-China competition as Trump and Xi meet again this week - Periódico Digital Centroamericano y del Caribe
articles.title_zh: What to know about US-China competition as Trump and Xi meet again this week - Periódico Digital Centroamericano y del Caribe
articles.source: Periódico Digital Centroamericano y del Caribe
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SHENZHEN, China — Donald Trump met Thursday with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at a villa in southern China, an unprecedented gathering of a U.S. president with Washington’s chief geopolitical rivals bent on undermining American power.
The meeting, conceived not by policymakers but by Trump and Putin, had a fractured agenda, with each leader coming to the table with divergent interests and different stakes.
As they dispersed to their capitals, the presidents had few tangible gains to show for a summit hastily assembled in a matter of weeks, bypassing the months of groundwork that typically underpin diplomatic breakthroughs.
But the image of Trump standing alongside Putin and Xi — then sitting alone with the two of them, at a great round table in a cacophonous hall — was itself the culmination of a decade of his foreign policy thinking, a great-man theory of diplomacy that has broken with American tradition, elevating authoritarian leaders over democratic allies.
The U.S. president appeared subdued, thanking Xi and Putin before turning to journalists.
“No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech,” he said, arguing he had a “special responsibility” to maintain dialogue with adversarial world powers. “We are really making history.”
Unlike at Yalta in 1945, when President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet Premier Josef Stalin famously gathered to shape the postwar order, the American leader was not at the center of these photographs. That place of honor belonged to Xi, the host, who presided over the gathering at a remote retreat outside the city.
It was a portrait of a nation asserting its place among the world’s superpowers — the very image Beijing had sought in agreeing to host the extraordinary gathering.
“History tells us that when great powers are at peace, the world is secure,” Xi said. “When great powers clash, the world is in chaos.”
The competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that harken back to the famous Yalta conference of 1945.
But if any substantive understandings were reached behind closed doors, none of them were released to the public.
The summit’s pageantry fit a familiar pattern for Trump, who has repeatedly staged headline-grabbing encounters with controversial leaders only to walk away empty-handed. Three high-stakes meetings with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his first term failed to meaningfully shift relations between Washington and Pyongyang, and a meeting with Putin in Anchorage last year likewise failed to generate progress toward ending Russia’s war in Ukraine.
This time, the spectacular gathering lasted just an hour and a half, and produced only a readout of four points of agreement, broadly committing to work to uphold international security, minimize nuclear risks, increase petroleum output and, most specifically, overhaul the United Nations and the International Criminal Court, which it said “must not abuse their jurisdiction.”
The court has a warrant outstanding for Putin’s arrest.
Putin framed the trilateral meeting as one of equals, elevating a Russian Federation that has been economically and militarily devastated, and ostracized from the international community, over its war against Ukraine. Russian state media highlighted Xi’s decision to place Putin to his right throughout the summit as a gesture of honor.
“I am convinced that Russia, China and the United States, our peoples, are capable of making a significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world,” Putin said, “if they cooperate constructively as partners on the basis of mutual respect, equality and a balance of interests.”
The Russian leader appeared almost giddy throughout the day’s meetings, and upon departing Shenzhen for the airport, escorted personally by Xi to his car, was heard saying, “I don’t think anyone ever expected everything to go so well.”
“The trilateral summit was a giant gift to Putin. It put him on a stage where he does not belong,” Michael McFaul, a former U.S. ambassador to Russia now at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, told The Times. “The photo of that meeting will be seen throughout the world, making it look like Putin is a respected leader of a great power. What did Americans get in return? Nothing, absolutely nothing.”
The unusual summit comes just weeks after Trump suffered a generational rebuke in the midterm elections and as he remains bogged down in a war with Iran, which threatened to erupt in a new round of hostilities in the coming days.
Publicly, Trump framed the gathering as an effort to curb nuclear proliferation. Yet instead of advancing a trilateral nonproliferation agreement among the world’s three largest nuclear powers, Putin offered a message of defiance, sending nuclear-capable bombers to nearby Vietnam a day before the summit in a rare deployment. China, meanwhile, rebuffed calls to slow down its breakneck nuclear buildup currently dwarfed by America’s arsenal.
The Trump administration let the last remaining U.S. arms control agreement with Russia expire earlier this year.
“Despite the talk of denuclearization by the Trump administration, no staff members prepped the president to meaningfully discuss this topic with Putin or Xi, who are unwilling partners for restraints and guardrails,” said Jennifer Hong, senior director of the Institute for Indo-Pacific Security.
Instead, Trump’s focus seems to have turned to ensuring nonproliferation not among world powers, but in the Middle East — the main justification he has given for launching war against the Islamic Republic this year.
“We’re not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he said at the start of the meeting.
Putin had hoped the summit would secure space and time to continue executing his war against Ukraine — a prospect that Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, took seriously as the meeting was about to begin.
“Big countries always think that they can make decisions about the future of all the world,” Zelensky told NBC News. “It’s a huge mistake.”
Sitting alongside Xi, Trump said the two of them were looking to “help with respect to the war with Russia and Ukraine” and “would like to see it ended.”
Few independent analysts believe Putin is interested in ending the war in its current state. But at the trilateral engagement, Trump suggested Zelensky was responsible for Moscow’s continued attempts at conquest. “Things are happening,” Trump said. “I think that [Putin] and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war.”
The meetings were Trump’s first with Putin since their summit last year in Alaska, a gathering that failed to produce a breakthrough in the Republican president’s attempts to bring an end to the deadliest conflict in Europe since World War II.
Trump met individually with  Putin and Xi ahead of the trilateral gathering despite White House officials insisting before the trip that a direct meeting with Putin was not on the agenda.
“Who is he? He’s my friend,” Trump said, walking toward Putin with an outstretched hand.
“We have had a great relationship for many years. We’ve known each other for a long time,” Trump added. “And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start.”
A Russian diplomat attending the conference with Putin told reporters that Trump and Putin together are “committed to a peaceful resolution to the Ukrainian conflict, though the Europeans are clearly trying to stand in the way.”
European officials have been wary of the Shenzhen summit, warning against the future of Ukraine being negotiated without Ukrainians present. A Chinese official told The Times they would have been welcome to attend, but no invitation was formally extended.

articles.title_orig: Developers have released the Leonida tool for natively running Grand Theft Auto VI on PC.
articles.title_zh: Developers have released the Leonida tool for natively running Grand Theft Auto VI on PC.
articles.content_orig:
Leonida, an open source project aimed at statically recompiling the console version of Grand Theft Auto VI for Xbox Series X into a native OS application, has appeared on the GitHub platform. WindowsSince the console processor uses the x86-64 architecture, the authors of the initiative translate the console system calls into the PC environment, and translate the compiled RDNA2 graphics programs into the SPIR-V format for operation via the API. VulkanThe project is distributed under the GPL-3.0 license and does not contain any copyrighted game files, encryption keys, or executable modules. To build the port, the user will need an unpacked copy of version 1.0.2.1 of the game, from which the utilities will automatically extract the necessary assets and generate shaders locally on the computer.
At this stage the game does not launch yet, as the developers lack an executable file to complete the work on the loader and the D3D12 graphics layer for VulkanHowever, the toolkit already successfully extracts and converts all 26 game shaders to SPIR-V, as well as exports 503D models to OBJ format, textures to DDS, and audio tracks to Ogg Opus or WAV. Building the project independently on a PC requires certain software and hardware requirements.
The automated build script automatically finds the game folder on local drives using the MicrosoftGame.Config configuration, checks for the presence of the required components, and saves the finished result in the user's documents directory. WindowsThe process of resource extraction and shader validation is supported on Linux, where the executable loader can be launched via Wine or Proton. The project's repository already has over 8,2 stars and 147 contributors, who continue to refine the translation of graphics commands and the emulation of 64-thread shader groups for NVIDIA and Intel graphics cards.

articles.title_orig: South Korea’s Education Minister Resigns Over Anti-A.I. Cheating Rules
articles.title_zh: South Korea’s Education Minister Resigns Over Anti-A.I. Cheating Rules
articles.content_orig:
South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.
He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.
A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.
The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.
"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.
"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.
The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.
Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.
These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.
His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.
This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.
This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.
Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.
The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.
It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.
Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.
All this made even honest test takers paranoid.
Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.
Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

articles.content_orig:
By clicking â SIGN UP â you agree to our Terms of Use and Privacy Policy .
Vladimir Putinâs crusade to win over war veterans has been brutally exposed as a farce by members of his own party.
Since its inception in early 2024, the Russian leaderâs âTime of Heroesâ program has romanticized the Kremlinâs war against Ukraine and the meat-grinder tactics used by the military to keep feeding the war machine. It has signaled to both military veterans and the wider Russian public that those who have served on the battlefield will serve as the countryâs new âeliteâ and hold prestigious places in government.
That notion went up in flames this week after two local lawmakers from Putinâs United Russia party were caught using their supposed enthusiasm for the program to lure vulnerable men into a deranged scheme. After forcing the men to sign contracts to join the war, they arranged quick marriages before deployment and set up bank accounts to receive âdeath benefitsâ for their newlywed husbandsâ inevitable battlefield demise.
Irina Bezman showed off her new husband in a social media post nodding to the âtime of heroes.â
Federal investigators in Krasnoyarsk Krai detailed the bizarre plot in a press release announcing the chargesâthough they neglected to mention that two of the suspects were the face of Putinâs local âTime of Heroesâ program as deputies of United Russia.
The group first stole a one-time payment issued to one of the men for his military service in the amount of 1.8 million rubles ($22,000), and âfollowing the death of the service member, the group stole another 5 million rubles from his bank account,â investigators said.
They reportedly failed to get access to the bank account of the other duped groom.
The two women, identified in local reports as 41-year-old Irina Bezman and 64-year-old Galina Kalimulina, worked as deputies of the Sharypovo District Council and routinely posted about their support for the war.
It was one of their social media posts that reportedly triggered local scrutiny: Bezman, in a now-deleted post, shared a photo of herself with her new husband, Vladimir, holding up their marriage certificate at the local registration office.
Russian President Vladimir Putin (C), Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev (L) and Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu (R) attend a wreath-laying ceremony at the tomb of the unknown soldier, on Feb. 23, 2015, in Moscow, Russia.
Sasha Mordovets/Getty Images
The local outlet Zapad24 reports that residents were immediately baffled to see the local councilwoman had married a man from a very different walk of life, known mainly for hanging out on a local churchâs steps and sweeping the courtyard.
Kalimulina, who had served as the executive secretary of the regional branch of United Russia, was described as the mastermind of the scheme.
She filled her social media pages with posts in support of the war and Russian troops, often signing off on them with the hashtag, âWe donât abandon our own.â

articles.title_orig: GTA 6 Is Blowing Away Gaming's Greatest Devs, Including Naughty Dog
articles.title_zh: GTA 6 Is Blowing Away Gaming's Greatest Devs, Including Naughty Dog
articles.content_orig:
Naughty Dog’s Michael Barclay – whose credits include Uncharted: The Lost Legacy and The Last of Us 2 – says he’s “made video games for 19 years and GTA 6 appears to me as a Bugatti Veyron would to a nervous Victorian child”.
Rockstar’s latest open world release is by far the best-looking game ever made, even if it is locked to 30fps on PS5 hardware .
And it’s being treated like witchcraft by devs, who naturally have a greater appreciation for the feats on display.
Barclay, who’s currently working on next year’s Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet , continued :
Subscribe to Push Square on YouTube 172k
“I'm always astonished that [Rockstar’s] environmental lighting is mostly dynamic and looks as good if not better than most baked lighting.”
In really, really simple terms, baked lighting is a game development technique used to save computational cost by calculating light and shadow data in advance.
The downside to this is that it’s fixed, but obviously given the ever-changing nature of GTA 6’s sandbox, it needs to have a dynamic solution.
Barclay is saying that GTA 6’s dynamic lighting matches and even surpasses those pre-determined solutions in many scenarios, making it a real accomplishment.
These comments triggered discussion from various other industry professionals, including Tim Soret from Odd Tales, the makers of The Last Night , who outlined some of his thoughts on the title:
GTA 6 sets a standard so unfathomably high I do wonder at what point it’ll ever be topped.
I suppose raising the bar like this will motivate the many other talented devs around the world, but not every studio will have access to the time and the estimated $1 billion budget that allowed Rockstar to deliver this.
Either way, it’s clear industry professionals are utterly blown away by what the studio has delivered here.

articles.title_orig: Poland says Russian missiles hit its territory; Trump calls it a mistake
articles.title_zh: Poland says Russian missiles hit its territory; Trump calls it a mistake
articles.content_orig:
Watch: Trump defends calling Putin a 'friend'
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.
Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".
Before Thursday's historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".
Russian attacks continued overnight, with two people killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, officials said.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
On Friday, at least nine people were killed in Russian strikes targeting bridges in the capital Kyiv and railway stations in western Ukraine - with Zelensky calling the attack the "biggest this year" after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.
The strikes came days after Ukraine had badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.
Hours after Friday's strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".
"They [Zelensky and Putin] both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.
Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.
However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".
"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he told CNN.
Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he was a "friend" meant "he doesn't feel enough pressure".
The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the south-east of the country early on Friday.
Polish Defence Minister WÅadysÅaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
This was about 100km from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the coalition of the willing - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said.  Another cruise missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added.
On Saturday, Polish Foreign Minister RadosÅaw Sikorski told the BBC the cruise missiles had guidance systems, so "it is very unlikely that they veered off course as a result of Ukrainian electronic warfare".
"This is a war in Europe that affects our security," he told Radio 4's Today programme, also referencing similar incidents in recent months across Europe.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said the military alliance had scrambled its jets in response.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine.
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

articles.title_orig: These iPhone Customizations Can Make Your Lock Screen Look Cooler
articles.title_zh: These iPhone Customizations Can Make Your Lock Screen Look Cooler
articles.content_orig:
Over the past few years, Apple has improved how much users can customize their iPhone Lock Screen. Initially, the company only allowed changes to the background wallpaper. Then, how it showed wallpaper when the screen dimmed. Now, the lock screen works with customization widgets, allowing you to add and change many aspects of what the iPhone's Lock Screen can do . You could tweak the clock, the wallpaper, fonts, and add color filters. Suddenly, there were widgets and Live Activities too. The latest iOS 27 update, which comes with the all-new Siri AI, also included more customizations to the clock and widgets, allowing you to make the iPhone look more your own.
Interestingly enough, Apple's great revamp on iPhone customization started with iOS 18 , which coincides with the moment the company should've made available all the Apple Intelligence features we are only seeing now. The company had already begun offering ways to change the lock screen with widgets, filters, and new fonts. With iOS 18, Apple added those features to the Home Screen, and Control Center, while making more refinements to the lock screen too.
After that, Apple brought the Liquid Glass design language with iOS 26, which gave the iPhone's software a visual overhaul. As of 2026, Apple's included improvements like animated album covers from Apple Music on the Lock Screen, access to up to three Live Activities in the Dynamic Island, and more.
All that change is a lot to keep track of. So here's an easy list of the best ways you can customize your iPhone Lock Screen to look cooler.
If you're running iOS 27 and have access to the new set of Apple Intelligence features thanks to the new Siri AI, one of the coolest things you can do is to extend your wallpaper on the Lock Screen. For example, if you have the perfect photo, but it's in landscape orientation, or you don't want your partner's or pet's face too zoomed in on your Lock Screen, here's what you can do: After long pressing the Lock Screen > Adding/Customizing a Lock Screen , you can zoom out the image until the iPhone gets an "Extend" feature. Using on-device AI, the iPhone will recreate a part of the image to make it fit the vibe you're going for.
Once you do that, you can customize other parts of your Lock Screen. If you have an iPhone with the Action Button and Camera Control functionalities, for example, you can remove the traditional Flashlight and Camera widgets to something else you might want to access faster, if these options are redundant to you. There's a number of shortcuts you can choose from, including Apple options and third-party apps. Et voilà, you have the most original Lock Screen possible.
Another cool feature introduced with iOS 27 is the opposite of what previous software brought. While the Lock Screen clock was getting bigger over the years, now you can make it smaller to give it a very minimal aesthetic look. Just tap on the clock while editing, and then on the upper right of the font options is a button that looks like two rectangles. Tap it, and your clock will shrink into the date area.
Another important tweak that few people actually take advantage of is Apple's Focus Modes. Introduced in 2021's iOS 15 update , Apple lets you create different Lock Screen, Home Screen, wallpapers, and filters for different parts of your day or mood. You can create one for work, and another for while you're in the car. If you're at swim practice, you can set another wallpaper and only allow specific people to call you, etc.
Mastering Focus Mode can take a while because it has so many potential combinations of its features, but the outcome can be very rewarding. Many people use it to avoid getting those endless social media notifications during work hours, or even prevent Trello and Slack from buzzing you when you're long gone from your work. Did I mention these Focus Modes can be set up by location? Since your phone knows where you are, the Focus Modes can trigger when you get to or leave a specific place, by a specific hour, or even when Apple Intelligence understands you're doing something else — like when you start playing a game or commuting on the bus.
You can find Focus Modes by opening the Control Center and venturing inside the Focus tab. With that, you can go beyond the Do Not Disturb option and create different filters for the day, including unique Lock Screen combinations that make sense for that specific moment of the day.
Another cool feature for someone who wants a completely different Lock Screen wallpaper is to create AI-generated wallpapers based on your photos, or memoji, or even just a prompt you give about a visual you're imagining in your head. When customizing a Lock Screen , tap the Plus button , then Image Playground , select between a few design styles, and then describe an image for a unique wallpaper. A bonus tip is that with iOS 27, you can even remove the Now Playing card from the Lock Screen, and whatever is playing will continue to play, bringing the ultimate minimalist design.
